d195af90bdb53500: LOS ANGELES: A buzzy new documentary about jailed tech CEO Elizabeth Holmes gave "Clayface," a gory Batman villain origin story, a run for its money at this weekend's domestic box office, industry estimates showed Sunday.

"Clayface," from Warner Bros. and DC Comics, debuted in first place with US$24 million in the US and Canada, but A24's "You Can See Everything" was not far behind at $20 million, according to Exhibitor Relations.

That represents the second biggest weekend ever for a documentary - after Fahrenheit 9/11 (2004) - and an "extremely rare" 28% increase from its debut the prior week, according to analyst David A. Gross of Franchise Entertainment Research.
The three-hour documentary, co-directed by comedian Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, follows Holmes and her family at home in 2023 during the month before she began an 11-year prison sentence.
Holmes was convicted of defrauding investors in her medical testing company Theranos after touting lofty promises she couldn't deliver.

The scandal fuelled a media circus and was chronicled in a book, multiple podcasts, and the biographical mini-series "The Dropout," starring Amanda Seyfried - who has sparked some awards chatter with her surprise cameo in "You Can See Everything."

The film has now earned an estimated total of US$45 million at the domestic box office, with some analysts predicting it could become the first documentary to be nominated for Best Picture at the Oscars.
Third place this week went to Fathom Events' animated film "Wildwood," which debuted at US$11 million after over a decade in production.
Made by the stop-motion animation studio behind 2009 hit "Coraline," "Wildwood" follows a young girl who must venture into an enchanted forest after her brother is whisked away by crows.
"Audiences love this movie, but it needs a very long run to recoup its costs, or an over-performance overseas, and neither appears likely," said Gross.
In fourth place, falling from first last week, was Paramount's "Street Fighter" at US$8.6 million.
Based on the beloved Capcom video game, "Street Fighter" follows super-powered martial artists competing in a global tournament who uncover and battle a sinister conspiracy.
Fifth place went to Black Bear's "Wicker," which debuted at US$5.8 million.
The film stars Olivia Colman as a lonely fisherwoman and Alexander Skarsgard as her fantastical husband made out of wicker, whose housework - and bedroom skills - quickly become the talk of the town.
Rounding out the top 10:
'Other Mommy' (US$3.9 million)
'Sense and Sensibility' (US$3.4 million)
'Whalefall' (US$3.2 million)
'Verity' (US$3.1 million)
'Resident Evil' (US$3.0 million)

358216ed3c5e035b: AUSTIN: Max Verstappen admitted he had the wrong tyre strategy and lacked pace as he hung on to claim third place for Red Bull in Sunday's United States Grand Prix.
The four-time world champion, who started from second on the grid, opened the race with two stints on soft tyres that left him with a lot of work to do as he was stuck with a two-stop strategy.

Runaway world championship leader Kimi Antonelli won convincingly for Mercedes ahead of Ferrari's Charles Leclerc and now needs only two points in Mexico next weekend to become F1's youngest champion.
Verstappen had hoped to compete with the 20-year-old Italian but was ultimately unable to match his overall speed and performance.
"I think our overall pace was not good enough and probably the tyres that we had available were not the right ones," he said.
"It's something that we have to understand because I think in the last few races it was always working well for us.

"For whatever reason it didn't work out here. And this choice of tyres also meant everyone knew we had to be on a two-stop race. We still managed to get on the podium, maybe a little bit luckily with the VSC (Virtual Safety Car) at the end, but I'll take it."

After two consecutive wins at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia and the Singapore Grand Prix it was a disappointment for Verstappen but it extended his strong run of results in the second half of the season.
It also meant the end of his slim hopes of fifth world championship title. --AFP
25e6c3356b6ae402: WELLINGTON: Voting opened in New Zealand on Monday for the Nov 7 general election, with ballot boxes available for nearly two weeks at shopping centres, transport hubs and community halls, ahead of what is expected to be a closely contested race.
The Electoral Commission said 207 voting places were open on Monday, with that number rising to more than 2,300 on election day. Overseas voting opened earlier, on Oct 21.

The race remains too close to call. Public polling has swung sharply in recent days, underscoring the absence of a clear frontrunner under New Zealand's mixed-member proportional system, where coalition deals are often needed to form a government.

A 1News-Verian poll published on October 20 put the ruling centre-right National Party at 32% and opposition Labour at 27%, while a Post/Freshwater Strategy poll published a day earlier had Labour narrowly ahead on 28.7% to National's 27.6%.
In both surveys, the smaller Opportunity party was polling around or above the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament, making it a potential kingmaker.
The start of voting comes just hours after enrolment closed at midnight on Sunday, a deadline that has become one of the campaign's most contentious issues.
Unlike in previous elections, voters can no longer enroll or update their details during the voting period, meaning people not enrolled by the cutoff cannot cast a vote in this election.

Critics say the earlier cutoff could deter participation, particularly among groups that are harder to reach. The Human Rights Commission said last year that ending election-day enrolment was likely to unjustifiably restrict participation and would disproportionately affect underrepresented groups.
As of Oct 21, 3,729,667 people were enrolled to vote, already above the final 2023 total of 3,688,292, when the enrolment rate was 94.7%, according to the Electoral Commission.
11ca3b0be0e58ef8: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia measures what its states produce. It does not yet adequately measure what they produce together.

We know the size of each state economy, its industries, household incomes and international trade. Less visible are the goods, services, workers, capital and knowledge crossing state boundaries before final output reaches the market.

This gap affects how Malaysia understands regional inequality, designs infrastructure and distributes development expenditure. State GDP identifies where value is created. It cannot, alone, explain how that value moves through the federation or reaches households.

Malaysia already publishes national input-output accounts and has valuable regional research. It needs a regularly updated, publicly accessible official framework measuring production flows between individual states.
States Apart, Factories Together

Penang and Kedah are separate jurisdictions but increasingly connected production locations. Bayan Lepas, Perai, Batu Kawan and Kulim draw upon overlapping suppliers, skills, logistics and multinational networks.

Penang contributes accumulated industrial capabilities. Kulim offers additional land, utilities and manufacturing capacity. Firms can expand while retaining access to Penang's ecosystem. This is a regional division of productive functions.

The Northern Corridor Implementation Authority has a statutory mandate to coordinate development across Penang, Kedah, Perlis and Perak. Better interstate production accounts would strengthen its decisions on infrastructure, supplier development and investment, helping establish what each state contributes and captures.
Penang accounted for 38.1 per cent of Malaysian exports in 2025. That demonstrates international exposure, without revealing purchases from Kedah or where the resulting wages and profits accrue.
Malaysia measures the corridor's transactions with the world more readily than the domestic relationships making them possible.

Industrial expansion also needs to deliver technological upgrading. More factories do not automatically create Malaysian intellectual property or stronger domestic ownership. The test is whether supplier capabilities deepen, firms enter higher-value activities and workers' incomes rise.
Output Is Not Household Prosperity
Sabah and Sarawak expose different weaknesses in the same statistical picture.

Sabah's economy grew by 5.1 per cent in 2025, yet manufacturing contributed only 7.2 per cent of state GDP, compared with Sarawak's 24.9 per cent and Penang's 47.3 per cent. Its challenge concerns the structure beneath growth.

When commodities leave Sabah for processing elsewhere, potential gains extend beyond factory margins. Testing, engineering, branding and supplier relationships accumulate where production occurs. Rebuilding those capabilities later is difficult.

Sabah needs commercially viable downstream production around palm oil, fisheries and food processing. Incentives should reward operating facilities, skilled jobs, local purchases and products delivered.

Sarawak's GDP per capita exceeded the national average in 2024. Yet its mean monthly household income was RM6,947, below Malaysia's RM9,155 that year. Annual output per person and monthly income per household are not directly comparable. The two comparisons nevertheless warrant investigating how production translates into residents' welfare.
They do not establish that profits are leaving Sarawak. Ownership, labour compensation, household composition and the destination of operating surpluses remain matters for investigation.

Sarawak's Global Supply Chain and Sourcing Programme connects anchor investors with local suppliers. Its success should be measured through procurement, contracts, technology transfer, wages and projects reaching commercial production. Durable economic relationships are the objective.

Production networks also explain vulnerability. Diesel connects plantations, harvesting crews, mills, ports and exports. Higher costs or shortages propagate through these chains, with distance and infrastructure shaping the regional burden.
Count Connections, Not Just Allocations

Budget 2027 supports initiatives including Kulim Hi-Tech Park, Sibu Special Economic Zone negotiations, Sabah's electricity projects and RM3.3 billion for roads in Sabah and Sarawak. Alongside the Perak–Penang bulk-water agreement, these form elements of a national production architecture.

Water security supports Penang's industry. Reliable electricity affects Sabah's capacity to industrialise. Roads can lower the cost of building Borneo supply chains. Their value extends beyond the jurisdiction where expenditure occurs.
Federal spending should therefore be judged by the connections it enables and the distribution of benefits, alongside allocations received.

The six less-developed states allocated RM21.26 billion in federal development expenditure cannot be treated as one category. Kedah needs deeper participation in advanced manufacturing networks; Sabah needs downstream capacity and reliable infrastructure; Sarawak needs stronger conversion of production into household prosperity.

Malaysia's New Incentive Framework shifts attention towards outcomes. Monitoring should include where suppliers, workers and research activities are located and whether investment strengthens domestic firms across state boundaries. Does a Penang project purchase inputs from Kedah? Does a Sarawak investment create local supplier contracts and skilled employment for resident workers?

Existing research offers a foundation. A January 2026 study by Pang Chun Sian and Mohd Khairul Hisyam Hassan constructs a 2015 interregional input-output table covering Sabah, Sarawak and Peninsular Malaysia, estimating flows across 30 sectors. This work should be extended and institutionalised. However, treating the peninsula as one region cannot reveal production relationships between its individual states.

The Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM) could build linked state and interregional accounts using administrative records and targeted surveys. A table linking states would show which industries buy from which locations, making interdependence visible. Estimates should be balanced, validated and published with uncertainty ranges. Policymakers need reliable answers to specific questions while more comprehensive accounts develop.

Three pilots would be useful: Penang–Kedah semiconductor dependence, Sabah's downstream-processing deficit and Sarawak's energy-transition exposure. Each should identify essential purchases by origin and destination, freight flows, supplier locations, commuting patterns and employment links.

Linking production accounts to social accounting matrices would help trace payments to workers, owners and households. Ownership, wage and income data could distinguish each state's contribution to production from the benefits retained by residents and test whether growth is narrowing regional disparities.

Comparable benefit-cost analysis should guide interstate electricity, water, transport and digital infrastructure. It must identify who finances shared assets, who benefits and where investment follows. Energy-transition gains and losses may occur in different states and affect different workers.
The federalism question concerns how states produce together and whether the gains are shared.
Malaysia already finances interstate production architecture. Its accounting framework should make those connections and their distributional consequences clearer.
Regional policy must move from counting allocations to measuring connections, and from celebrating output to examining household prosperity.
Malaysia's economic map is not empty. It is incomplete. The task is to draw the missing lines.

Economist Samirul Ariff Othman is an international relations analyst and a senior consultant with Global Asia Consulting (GAC). Samirul has a background as a senior researcher at the Malaysian Institute of Economic Research. The viewpoints articulated are solely those of the author.

d9d4c0025d17076b: KUALA LUMPUR: Rising building material prices are putting pressure on property developers to protect profit margins without pricing homebuyers out of the market, as industry players grapple with reported increases of 20 per cent to 30 per cent in selected construction inputs.

However, the impact on overall project costs varies depending on the materials used, their contribution to total construction expenses and developers' ability to negotiate competitive procurement terms, according to Mah Sing Group Bhd founder and group managing director Tan Sri Leong Hoy Kum.
Leong said the group's overall construction costs had increased by an estimated 5.0 per cent to 10 per cent, significantly below the reported price hikes for certain building materials.
He attributed this to the group's emphasis on value engineering, economies of scale and long-standing supplier relationships, which help it manage expenses while maintaining its product positioning.

The approach is particularly important as Mah Sing continues to focus on homes priced between RM300,000 and RM700,000, with selected offerings extending to RM800,000, catering to buyers seeking affordability without compromising on quality.
Leong said the reported 20 per cent to 30 per cent increase in building material prices over the past year was a general industry estimate and did not reflect the group's own experience.

"Some materials may have experienced significant price hikes, but their actual contribution to total construction costs could be relatively small," he told Business Times on the sidelines of the opening of the M Mira sales gallery in Setapak, recently.

He said a sharp increase in the price of an individual material did not necessarily translate into a comparable rise in a project's overall construction budget, as the impact depended on its share of total costs.
Materials such as cement, steel and sand form part of the construction cost structure, but their respective contributions vary across projects.
Materials with a relatively small cost base, for instance, could record steep percentage increases without significantly changing the overall construction bill, Leong said.

To manage these pressures, Mah Sing incorporates value engineering from the initial design stage, enabling its teams to optimise layouts, specifications and construction methods while maintaining the intended product quality.
"We practise value engineering from day one, ensuring that our designs are planned efficiently to manage costs," he said.
The group also draws on its established supplier network and long-standing relationships to secure competitive terms.
As a large customer, Mah Sing benefits from purchasing scale and its reputation as a reliable payer, strengthening its bargaining position with suppliers, Leong said.

He added that several departments worked together to monitor expenses and maintain tight control over project budgets, allowing the group to identify potential cost pressures early and manage them throughout the development process.

The distinction between individual material price movements and overall construction costs is increasingly important for developers, particularly those targeting first-time homebuyers and middle-income households, where affordability remains a key consideration.
According to the Real Estate and Housing Developers' Association (Rehda) Malaysia, construction costs rose by an average of 13 per cent in the first half of 2026.

Rehda president Datuk Zaini Yusoff said earthworks and infrastructure costs had increased by between 20 per cent and 30 per cent, while normal building works recorded increases of 3.0 per cent to 5.0 per cent.

The divergent cost movements highlight the uneven pressure across different construction components, with developers having to contend with higher expenses in specific areas while managing overall project budgets.

Olive Tree Property Consultants founder and chief executive officer Samuel Tan said developers faced a difficult balancing act as higher construction costs threatened to erode margins, while passing the increases on to buyers risked weakening demand.
Developers must therefore manage both their cost structures and selling prices to keep projects commercially viable, he told Business Times when contacted.
For Mah Sing, Leong said maintaining cost discipline was central to preserving its position in the mass-market and mid-market residential segments.

He said the group's focus on homes priced between RM300,000 and RM700,000 reflects its strategy of catering to buyers seeking relatively affordable properties, while retaining flexibility to offer selected units priced up to RM800,000.

"The group's ability to contain construction cost increases below the reported industry material price movements could provide some buffer against cost volatility, although the extent of the benefit will depend on future material prices, labour costs and the requirements of individual projects."

Looking ahead to 2027, Leong said Mah Sing would remain focused on its existing property development strategy, with cost management and affordability continuing to guide its growth plans amid an evolving construction cost environment.

46519bb6fe4849c0: PETALING JAYA: After learning she had breast cancer, Tan Chiew Mei cried through the night. Pregnant with her second child and with a young daughter at home, she could not stop wondering who would look after her daughter if she were no longer there.
Then she focused on two things: “I want to get treated. And I want to keep my baby.”

Tan, then 37, had found a hard lump in her breast. An initial ultrasound left her feeling reassured, but another assessment two weeks later found that it had grown, leading to a biopsy. The diagnosis was triple-negative breast cancer.
Chemotherapy began within days. With appointments and decisions coming quickly, she concentrated on getting through treatment. But knowing what to ask was another matter.
Tan was not too shy to speak, but often she simply could not think of a question during consultations. She would listen, say “OK”, and then draw a blank when invited to ask more.

She trusted her doctors with major treatment decisions, but that did not mean she understood every change she experienced along the way. Looking back, she encourages patients to prepare for appointments and raise even the questions that might seem unimportant.
No question too small

For women diagnosed with breast cancer during pregnancy, treatment decisions can feel especially difficult because the patient would be worrying about both her own health and her baby’s wellbeing, says consultant clinical oncologist Dr John Low.
The treatment plan has to consider both mother and baby, he explained, with close coordination between the oncology team, obstetrician and breast surgeon.

As not all cancer medicines are suitable during pregnancy, timing, monitoring and each woman’s circumstances all matter. Low encourages patients to understand what treatment is intended to achieve, why it has been recommended, how long it may take, possible side effects, and what to watch for at home.

Patients can also ask what the cancer type and stage mean specifically for them. Those conversations need not happen only at the first appointment; different concerns often emerge as treatment progresses.
Support beyond medication matters, too. Low encourages patients to ask about counselling, psychological support and patient groups that may help them through the experience.
“There are no questions that you cannot ask your treatment team,” he stressed.
For Tan, one of the hardest moments came after childbirth - she endured an induced delivery followed by surgery the next morning.
Waking weak and in pain, she cried again. “I felt very emotional, when I realised how difficult it had been to get to this point, and the journey was not over yet.”
There was now a newborn to care for alongside her older daughter, and more chemotherapy ahead. She also had to come to terms with being unable to breastfeed her son during treatment.

Some aspects of chemotherapy were easier than she had feared: she could eat and did not vomit. But other symptoms were difficult: she lost her hair, and experienced leg pain and tingling that made walking hard, as well as sore gums and itchy skin.
These were not minor inconveniences: they shaped daily life and deserved attention alongside the bigger medical decisions.
Who can help between appointments?
Oncology nurse educator Norhaniza Rashid hears many everyday concerns from patients, often only after a consultation, when they begin thinking about what treatment will mean once they are back home.

Before the first chemotherapy cycle, she tries to include a caregiver when explaining what to expect. Patients receive a great deal of information and may not remember all of it, so she checks in during later cycles and encourages them to contact the team during office hours.

Some ask whether they can still hug their children or share a bed with a spouse. Norhaniza reassures them that chemotherapy does not mean they must stop being close to their families, while explaining any precautions they should take at home.
It is just as important, she said, to know who to contact between appointments, which symptoms need urgent attention, and what to do outside office hours.

Fortunately, Tan had help outside the clinic. Her husband accompanied her to appointments, her mother cooked during chemotherapy, and her siblings helped care for the children. Her employer also checked the company’s prolonged-illness leave policy, allowing her time away from work.
“Whenever there was a doctor’s appointment, the whole village would come to my house,” she recalled.

Tan found distraction in K-dramas and, when she felt able, did light chores around the house to keep herself occupied. She also remembers patients swapping experiences in the waiting area, where conversation helped her feel part of a community.
Coping, however, did not mean she never felt overwhelmed.

Norhaniza encourages patients to do something they enjoy, such as gardening or catching up with friends. When someone cannot face even those suggestions, she asks what is worrying them most and listens patiently to offer the best advice.
So, what comes next?

Now a mother of three, Tan continues to attend follow-up appointments and says her checks have remained clear so far. Her approach to the possibility of recurrence is simply to “deal with it as it comes”.
The end of treatment brings its own set of questions: what follow-up is needed, which changes should be reported, and where to turn if concerns arise between visits.

Tan also wishes she had sought advice sooner when she first noticed the lump, rather than waiting for her next pregnancy appointment. She urges women not to take their health for granted, to be disciplined about breast self-awareness, and not to put off screening or having an unfamiliar change checked.
Her advice is simple: “Just ask whatever. Don’t feel shy to ask.”
8ed61d6f5433a7d0: PETALING JAYA: PAS's denial that seat negotiations with Barisan Nasional for the Melaka state election have been finalised raises doubts among analysts over the possible cooperation between the two in the 16th general election (GE16).
Syaza Shukri of International Islamic University Malaysia said Melaka was supposed to be a litmus test for cooperation between the coalition and the Islamic party.
"All is definitely not well. The fact that PAS has publicly said the seat distribution has not been finalised speaks volumes.
"Melaka is supposed to be the 'experiment' to gauge if they can work together or not. So this is not a good sign," she told FMT.
On Wednesday, BN chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said the coalition would contest 21 of Melaka's 28 state seats, while PAS and its allies would vie for the remaining seven.
However, PAS secretary-general Takiyuddin Hassan said the seat distribution had yet to be finalised, although he maintained that cooperation between the parties was certain.
Syaza said PAS's decision to publicly challenge the arrangement was significant, particularly as Zahid was unlikely to backtrack.
"BN will not back down, PAS doesn't seem happy with only seven.”
She said BN and PAS could end up facing off in some seats while maintaining cordial relations and focusing their attacks on Pakatan Harapan, similar to their approach in Johor.
Similarly, Azmi Hassan of Nusantara Academy said Melaka would be a crucial test for BN-PAS cooperation ahead of GE16, unlike Johor and Negeri Sembilan, where he believed cooperation was easier.
He said the problem in Melaka was not just the number of seats offered to PAS and Wawasan, but their chances of winning them.
Based on Zahid’s remarks, PAS and Wawasan would contest four DAP strongholds – Kota Laksamana, Kesidang, Bandar Hilir and Ayer Keroh.
"Wresting those seats from DAP would be a formidable challenge,” Azmi said.
Of the remaining three seats, Bukit Katil was represented by former chief minister Adly Zahari for two terms while Sungai Udang and Bemban seats were won by Bersatu in the last state election.
Mazlan Ali of Universiti Teknologi Malaysia believed that forming an alliance for GE16 would be challenging for Umno and PAS based on the current impasse in seat negotiations for the Melaka polls.
He said if PAS and Umno could not compromise in Melaka, it would also be difficult for the two parties to agree on seats in states led by the Islamic party.
Still, Mazlan felt that BN would want to work with PAS in Melaka, even though the coalition could win it on its own.
“BN wants to minimise the impact of split votes in Malay-majority areas.”
764396fba1a7bb16: PETALING JAYA: Penafian PAS rundingan pembahagian kerusi dengan Barisan Nasional (BN) bagi PRN Melaka sudah dimuktamadkan menimbulkan persoalan dalam kalangan penganalisis mengenai kemungkinan kedua-duanya bekerjasama pada PRU16.
Syaza Shukri daripada Universiti Islam Antarabangsa Malaysia berkata PRN Melaka sepatutnya menjadi ujian untuk melihat sama ada BN dan PAS mampu bekerjasama dengan baik.
“Jelas sekali ada perkara yang tidak kena. Hakikat bahawa PAS secara terbuka menyatakan pembahagian kerusi belum dimuktamadkan membawa makna yang besar.
“Melaka sepatutnya menjadi ‘eksperimen’ untuk mengukur sama ada mereka boleh bekerjasama atau tidak. Jadi, perkembangan ini bukan petanda yang baik,” katanya kepada FMT.
Rabu lalu, Pengerusi BN Zahid Hamidi berkata gabungan itu akan bertanding di 21 daripada 28 kerusi DUN Melaka, manakala PAS dan sekutunya akan bertanding di baki tujuh kerusi.
Bagaimanapun, Setiausaha Agung PAS Takiyuddin Hassan berkata pembahagian kerusi itu masih belum dimuktamadkan, walaupun menegaskan kerjasama antara kedua-dua pihak tetap akan berlaku.
Syaza berkata tindakan PAS mempertikaikan secara terbuka pengaturan itu sesuatu yang signifikan, terutama kerana Zahid dilihat sukar untuk mengubah pendiriannya.
“BN tidak akan berundur, manakala PAS pula nampaknya tidak berpuas hati dengan hanya tujuh kerusi.”

Menurutnya, BN dan PAS mungkin akhirnya bertembung di beberapa kerusi tetapi masih mengekalkan hubungan baik serta menumpukan serangan terhadap Pakatan Harapan (PH), seperti pendekatan mereka di Johor.

Sementara itu, Azmi Hassan daripada Akademi Nusantara berkata PRN Melaka akan menjadi ujian penting kepada kerjasama BN-PAS menjelang PRU16, berbeza dengan Johor dan Negeri Sembilan yang menurutnya lebih mudah untuk kedua-dua pihak mencapai persefahaman.
Katanya, masalah di Melaka bukan sekadar jumlah kerusi yang diberikan kepada PAS dan Wawasan, tetapi turut membabitkan peluang mereka untuk menang.
Berdasarkan kenyataan Zahid, PAS dan Wawasan dijangka bertanding di empat kubu kuat DAP, iaitu Kota Laksamana, Kesidang, Bandar Hilir dan Ayer Keroh.
“Mengambil alih kerusi itu daripada DAP bukan tugas mudah,” kata Azmi.
Daripada baki tiga kerusi, Bukit Katil diwakili bekas ketua menteri Adly Zahari selama dua penggal, manakala Sungai Udang dan Bemban dimenangi Bersatu pada PRN lalu.

Mazlan Ali daripada Universiti Teknologi Malaysia pula berpandangan usaha membentuk kerjasama bagi menghadapi PRU16 akan menjadi lebih sukar buat Umno dan PAS jika kebuntuan rundingan kerusi di Melaka berterusan.
Katanya, jika PAS dan Umno gagal mencapai kompromi di Melaka, kedua-dua parti juga mungkin berdepan kesukaran untuk mencapai persetujuan mengenai pembahagian kerusi di negeri yang diterajui PAS.
Bagaimanapun, Mazlan percaya BN masih mahu bekerjasama dengan PAS di Melaka walaupun gabungan itu berupaya memenangi negeri tersebut tanpa bantuan parti berkenaan.
“BN mahu mengurangkan kesan perpecahan undi di kawasan majoriti Melayu.”
1727d54fe927838f: ORLÉANS, France: Wrapped in the French tricolour, Loic Le Tourneau was among thousands of supporters who flocked on Sunday to see far-right leader Marine Le Pen officially launch her presidential campaign.
Outside the arena in the city of Orleans, fans milled about, tucking into hot dogs and French fries and snapping up Le Pen-branded T-shirts and scarves before heading inside.
But behind the festive atmosphere lay deep-seated anxieties about France's future among the roughly 8,500 people who turned out to hear the leader of the nationalist, anti-immigration party.

Le Tourneau, who travelled nearly an hour to attend the rally, said he was increasingly worried about insecurity in France – even though he said he had not experienced it firsthand in the countryside where he lives.
"I'm afraid because things have been deteriorating enormously for about ten years now," the 25-year-old told AFP.
"I'm worried things will keep getting worse if the National Rally doesn't come to power next year."
Polls show Le Pen – who has already made three unsuccessful presidential bids – is the frontrunner in the race to succeed centrist President Emmanuel Macron in next year's election.

But critics accuse her Eurosceptic party of remaining fundamentally racist despite her efforts to distance it from the legacy of her father, who co-founded what was then called the National Front and was convicted over racist and antisemitic remarks.
Her campaign launch came after weeks of unrest across France, where largely peaceful mass demonstrations have at times descended into violence and looting not seen in years.
Accusing Macron's centrist government of being soft on violent protesters, Le Pen vowed on Sunday to "restore the rule of law."
For Jacques Olivier, 65, a longtime supporter of the National Front then the National Rally, the stakes could hardly be higher.
"Marine has to win, otherwise France will collapse," said Olivier, who came from the Paris region.
He blamed immigration in part for what he saw as rising crime and violence.
"When you open the borders to the entire world, you get some not very nice people coming into our country to take advantage of us and to loot," he said, calling for "radical change."
"We have nothing to lose and everything to gain," he added.
-'WE'RE GOING TO WIN'-
Le Pen is running for the top job after an appeals court earlier this year upheld a graft conviction against her, but shortened a ban on her holding public office.
The choice of Orleans was a symbolic one: Joan of Arc lifted an English siege there in 1429 before being burned at the stake two years later.
Le Pen invoked the Catholic warrior – revered by the far right as a symbol of national resistance – in her speech, recalling how she had freed the city from a "foreign threat."
Among those drawn to Le Pen's message was Marie, a 19-year-old supporter with two French flags poking out of her handbag, who wanted a tougher stance on immigration.
"Those who love France should stay, and those who don't should leave," she said, declining to give her surname.
She also believed Le Pen would put an end to the "appalling" violence that has marred recent protests.
"There wouldn't be any more violent demonstrations," she said.
Yet despite the bleak picture supporters painted of France's current situation, the mood inside the arena was one of optimism.
Throughout the evening, the crowd repeatedly erupted into chants of "We're going to win! We're going to win!"--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd
d661a02afc7678aa: MONACO: Lille were made to pay for Tanguy Nianzou's red card as Monaco fought back to hold them to a 1-1 draw in Ligue 1 on Sunday, opening the door for Rennes to take the summit of the table thanks to a 3-0 win over struggling Strasbourg.

With Paris Saint-Germain and Lyon's match pushed back to Monday due to protests taking place across France this weekend, a winner in the principality would have gone three points clear at the top of the table.
But Lille have to content themselves with second spot on goal difference in the standings ahead of Monaco as both sides moved to 15 points – one ahead of Lyon, reigning champions PSG and Paris FC.
Rennes then took full advantage of the draw as they eased past 16th-placed Strasbourg in Brittany to climb to 16 points.

At the Stade Louis II, Ethan Mbappe's goal midway through the first period put Lille in the driving seat but a straight red for Nianzou just after the hour was swiftly punished by Edan Diop as the hosts forced a draw.
"The plan worked well in the first half," Lille coach Davide Ancelotti said.
"We managed to stick together," he added of his side following the dismissal of Nianzou.
"The mood in the dressing room is positive because we held on until the end."

The younger brother of France and Real Madrid star Kylian showed the crisp finishing instincts associated with the Mbappe name as he darted into the box and whipped a first-time shot with his left foot past Lukas Hradecky on 24 minutes.

Monaco rarely threatened through the rest of the opening period but the match burst into life in the second half as Monaco's Paris Brunner passed up a golden opportunity in the 65th minute, before Lille defender Nianzou was given his marching orders for a reckless challenge.
The hosts then levelled in the 74th minute as Diop's cross toward Brunner evaded everyone and nestled in the far corner.
First-half goals for Boulaye Dia and Sebastian Szymanski put Rennes in the driving seat against Strasbourg.
Polish midfielder Szymanski netted just after the hour to secure the points for Franck Haise's team as they moved into top spot in Ligue 1.

That situation could change on Monday when PSG take on Lyon, although Luis Enrique's team will be without Ballon d'Or winner Ousmane Dembele, captain Marquinhos and winger Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, who suffered an anterior cruciate ligament tear during the team's 4-2 Champions League victory against Barcelona in midweek.
Elsewhere on Sunday, eighth-placed Marseille held on to beat bottom-of-the-table Le Havre 4-3 at the Stade Velodrome.
The home side were cruising at 4-0 up with just under 15 minutes remaining, until a Josh Maja brace either side of a Lamine Ndiaye goal set up a grandstand finale.
Toulouse and Troyes, as well as Angers and Lorient, played out goalless stalemates, while Auxerre drew 1-1 with Le Mans.--AFP
0291d5aae1c95ff0: ALGIERS: Algeria on Sunday approved sending troops to neighbouring Niger to protect energy facilities, according to statements from both houses of parliament, in what is the country's first foreign deployment of military forces since the 1970s.
The rare measure comes as Algiers and Niamey strengthen security ties after moving earlier this year to repair strained relations and following a thwarted mutiny in Niger in August.
The overseas deployment will be a first since Algiers sent troops to support Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war.
The upper house approved the proposal, it said in a statement, with a legislator telling AFP it was approved by all 148 members in attendance.
The parliament's lower house said it also voted "by an absolute majority" to deploy the military unit in Niger, though it did not provide numbers.
Niger faces persistent attacks by armed groups, including in areas near the border with Algeria.
The neighbours, who share a 960-kilometre desert border, have agreed to deepen cooperation against jihadist violence, cross-border crime and trafficking.

"This decision marks a historic break with Algeria's doctrine of non-intervention in military conflicts beyond its borders," said Abdellah Akir, an international relations researcher, before the official confirmation.
"It's driven by the need to protect Algeria's strategic depth in the Sahel and to secure the future trans-Saharan gas pipeline," Akir told AFP.
The two countries have been working to build the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline (TSGP), a vast project to export natural gas to Europe from Nigeria via Niger.
'Strong signal'
Akir said the measure also sought to "send a strong signal to competing actors, including Morocco and the United Arab Emirates" -- two countries with which Algiers no longer has diplomatic ties.
Geoff Porter, an analyst with the North Africa Risk Consulting group, said the move was "illustrative of a shift in Algerian policy".
Algeria "had tried to maintain its national interests and exert its regional influence through its customary means -- dialogue, international law, multilateral forums," Porter told AFP.
"But in a multipolar and transactional world, those don't work anymore. Instead, Algeria moved toward more tangible means -- actual physical presence."
"Algeria is still committed to its foreign policy principles," he added. "It's just demonstrating them in a new way."
Earlier this month, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune signalled the possibility of military involvement in the Sahel country.
"We will protect Niger no matter what," he said in a televised address on Oct 3. "There are countries, which I will not name, that have conspired against (Niger). We stand by its side."
"Today, we have interests," Tebboune then said. "We have reached agreements (with Niger) in the oil, mining and other sectors, and some are seeking to destroy all of this overnight."
The deployment of troops outside Algeria's territory required the approval of two-thirds of its parliament, according to a constitutional amendment from 2020.
Gifted warplanes
The vote followed a visit last Wednesday by Niger's Defence Minister Salifou Modi to Algeria, where he met with Tebboune and army chief Said Chengriha.
A military cooperation protocol was signed by the two sides, according to Algerian reports, but no details were given at the time.
The move also comes months after Algiers gifted four military helicopters to Niamey.
The warplanes were deployed at the request of Nigerien authorities, the Algerian defence ministry said.
Additionally, Algeria inaugurated a 40-megawatt power plant in June intended to supply electricity to Niamey and surrounding areas.
Algeria and Niger's relations had been strained for months following Algeria's downing last year of a drone from Mali.
The incident triggered a diplomatic row, with Niger joining fellow junta-led allies Mali and Burkina Faso in recalling its ambassador from Algiers.
Algeria and Mali have since resumed diplomatic ties.
Niger has been run by General Abdourahamane Tiani since a July 2023 coup that toppled the elected president Mohamed Bazoum, who has been detained ever since.
f453384bdde2151d: AUSTIN: Max Verstappen admitted he had the wrong tyre strategy and lacked pace as he hung on to claim third place for Red Bull in Sunday’s United States Grand Prix.
The four-time world champion, who started from second on the grid, opened the race with two stints on soft tyres that left him with a lot of work to do as he was stuck with a two-stop strategy.

Runaway world championship leader Kimi Antonelli won convincingly for Mercedes ahead of Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc and now needs only two points in Mexico next weekend to become F1’s youngest champion.
Verstappen had hoped to compete with the 20-year-old Italian but was ultimately unable to match his overall speed and performance.
"I think our overall pace was not good enough and probably the tyres that we had available were not the right ones," he said.
"It's something that we have to understand because I think in the last few races it was always working well for us.

"For whatever reason it didn't work out here. And this choice of tyres also meant everyone knew we had to be on a two-stop race. We still managed to get on the podium, maybe a little bit luckily with the VSC (Virtual Safety Car) at the end, but I'll take it.”

After two consecutive wins at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia and the Singapore Grand Prix it was a disappointment for Verstappen but it extended his strong run of results in the second half of the season.
It also meant the end of his slim hopes of fifth world championship title.
797321c28311a98c: ORLEANS: Wrapped in the French tricolour, Loic Le Tourneau was among thousands of supporters who flocked on Sunday to see far-right leader Marine Le Pen officially launch her presidential campaign.
Outside the arena in the city of Orleans, fans milled about, tucking into hot dogs and French fries and snapping up Le Pen-branded T-shirts and scarves before heading inside.
But behind the festive atmosphere lay deep-seated anxieties about France's future among the roughly 8,500 people who turned out to hear the leader of the nationalist, anti-immigration party.

Le Tourneau, who travelled nearly an hour to attend the rally, said he was increasingly worried about insecurity in France - even though he said he had not experienced it firsthand in the countryside where he lives.
"I'm afraid because things have been deteriorating enormously for about ten years now," the 25-year-old told AFP.
"I'm worried things will keep getting worse if the National Rally doesn't come to power next year."
Polls show Le Pen - who has already made three unsuccessful presidential bids - is the frontrunner in the race to succeed centrist president Emmanuel Macron in next year's election.

But critics accuse her Eurosceptic party of remaining fundamentally racist despite her efforts to distance it from the legacy of her father, who co-founded what was then called the National Front and was convicted over racist and antisemitic remarks.
Her campaign launch came after weeks of unrest across France, where largely peaceful mass demonstrations have at times descended into violence and looting not seen in years.
Accusing Macron's centrist government of being soft on violent protesters, Le Pen vowed on Sunday to "restore the rule of law".
For Jacques Olivier, 65, a longtime supporter of the National Front then the National Rally, the stakes could hardly be higher.
"Marine has to win, otherwise France will collapse," said Olivier, who came from the Paris region.
He blamed immigration in part for what he saw as rising crime and violence.
"When you open the borders to the entire world, you get some not very nice people coming into our country to take advantage of us and to loot," he said, calling for "radical change".
"We have nothing to lose and everything to gain," he added.
-'We're going to win'- Le Pen is running for the top job after an appeals court earlier this year upheld a graft conviction against her, but shortened a ban on her holding public office.
The choice of Orleans was a symbolic one: Joan of Arc lifted an English siege there in 1429 before being burned at the stake two years later.
Le Pen invoked the Catholic warrior -- revered by the far right as a symbol of national resistance -- in her speech, recalling how she had freed the city from a "foreign threat".
Among those drawn to Le Pen's message was Marie, a 19-year-old supporter with two French flags poking out of her handbag, who wanted a tougher stance on immigration.
"Those who love France should stay, and those who don't should leave," she said, declining to give her surname.
She also believed Le Pen would put an end to the "appalling" violence that has marred recent protests.
"There wouldn't be any more violent demonstrations," she said.
Yet despite the bleak picture supporters painted of France's current situation, the mood inside the arena was one of optimism.
Throughout the evening, the crowd repeatedly erupted into chants of "We're going to win! We're going to win!"
352e06bc9a5b1de3: BELGRADE: Serbia's student-led movement declared victory in parliamentary elections Sunday ending 14 years in power for Aleksandar Vucic's right-wing populist party.
The victory in the snap vote comes after nearly two years of anti-government protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a canopy at Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.
The disaster has been widely blamed on corruption and triggered some of Serbia's largest protests since the fall of strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000.
"Preliminary results show that students are convincingly leading in almost all polling stations," Radomir Saicic, a candidate for the Students' List, said in a speech at the movement's election HQ.
"Students won and with them also a hope that Serbia can be a country of justice, freedom and dignity."
Voters cast ballots in huge numbers on Sunday, with the country recording its highest parliamentary election turnout in more than three decades.

Vucic conceded defeat less than two hours after polls closed, triggering raucous scenes in the capital as supporters of the movement celebrated the defeat of a government they blamed for deep-rooted corruption.
"I feel incredible," student Mila Martic told AFP from the List's headquarters. "I feel as though I am finally living in a free country."
Thousands poured into the capital's streets to celebrate the victory, with passing cars honking, crowds chanting, and fireworks lighting up the skyline.
According to the country's election officials, nearly 65% of its 6.4 million registered voters had cast their ballots by 6pm, two hours before polls closed.
The figure surpassed the 1993 parliamentary election, when just over 61% voted.
'Dream has come true'
During his speech to supporters, Vucic said preliminary figures suggested the student movement could win between 135 and 140 seats, handing it an outright majority in the 250-seat parliament.
The 56-year-old statesman, who has maintained close ties with Russia throughout his tenure, blamed foreign powers for the result.

"I want people to know, this was the validation of a revolution carried out with the direct support of various European countries and the US deep state, the one that is also against President Trump," he said.
For nearly two years, students have staged rallies and marched across the Balkan nation to reach voters directly and counter the media machine of Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party.
Their protests have drawn huge crowds, a final pre-election rally in Belgrade on Thursday attracting around 150,000 people, according to an independent protest monitor.
"A two-year-long dream has come true," Mirjana Nikolic, a candidate on the Students' List, said shortly after the win was announced.
Political novices
Most of the student list's 250 candidates are experts from fields including academia and the arts with little political experience.
The movement has a broad platform, centred on a pledge to fight corruption.
It evolved from demands for a transparent investigation into the Novi Sad tragedy into calls for an early election.
Despite pushing back against the movement for almost two years, Vucic under mounting pressure, called the vote last month, citing "major turbulence on the domestic political scene".
The right-wing populist leader resigned the presidency to run for prime minister.
Domestic and international observers were monitoring the vote, with students mobilising large numbers of volunteers to oversee the process.
03399c94c6f0ed23: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 26 — Keeping windows and doors shut during haze can help limit polluted air entering homes, but it may not be enough to protect occupants from fine particles that seep indoors, two indoor air quality specialists said.

Syida Nasri, Airscan’s head of indoor air quality and a Department of Occupational Safety and Health-accredited indoor air quality assessor, said fine particulate matter measuring 2.5 micrometres or less (PM2.5) could enter homes through gaps around windows, doors and other openings, even when they were kept closed.
“Merely staying indoors isn’t enough to protect against the haze,” she said.
PM2.5 is of particular concern because the particles are small enough to penetrate deep into the lungs and, unlike larger particles, can stay suspended in the air for long periods.

Syida said PM2.5 levels in closed homes averaged about half those outdoors, but these fine particles can cause inflammation, while ultrafine particles may enter the bloodstream and raise health risks.
“You won’t feel any of it, and you wouldn’t even know you’re being exposed without an indoor air quality sensor,” she said.

However, Applied Air Quality Specialists Sdn Bhd chief executive Tan Zhi Shen said most households could manage without an air purifier, particularly if occupants had no existing respiratory conditions or unusual sensitivities.
Tan said the bigger concern was larger particles such as PM10 and PM5, which he linked to coughing, adding that the need for a purifier depended on factors such as a home’s size and layout.
The two specialists differed on how much protection ordinary homes could provide, but agreed that residents should monitor indoor air quality and cut avoidable sources of pollution.
Keep the haze out, but know when to ventilate
Ventilation is normally important because cooking, cleaning and bathing introduce pollutants and moisture into a home, but during heavy haze the priority is to keep outdoor pollution out, Syida said.
“But we need to flip this during a heavy haze. Stop the bleeding first,” she said.
She said closing windows and doors reduces exposure but does not create an airtight barrier, so residents should not assume that staying inside eliminates the risk.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Md Noor Bujang watches TV at his home in Rawang, Selangor, on October 16, while using an oxygen concentrator. Specialists say staying indoors with the aircon running does not guarantee clean air during haze. — AFP pic
Keeping a home shut for long periods, however, lets indoor pollutants build up.
“Your house is constantly emitting things: chemicals from your cleaning products, smoke and grease from cooking, moisture from everyday living,” she said.
In Malaysia’s hot and humid climate, trapped moisture can also encourage mould growth.

Syida advised opening windows when outdoor air improves, such as after rain or when wind clears the haze, and cutting back on frying, smoky cooking and strong cleaning detergents while windows are shut.
Both specialists said burning incense, candles or cigarettes indoors would worsen matters, with Syida noting that incense could be a significant source of particulate pollution.
Kitchen hoods and bathroom exhaust fans that vent outdoors also call for caution, as the air they expel must be replaced, potentially drawing polluted air in through gaps.
Both specialists also urged residents to monitor indoor air quality rather than judge by whether haze is visible outside.
“You measure it,” Syida said, adding, “I always tell people air quality measurement is like illuminating a dark room.”
She said even an inexpensive monitor could show trends, although its readings might not be accurate in absolute terms.
Does air-conditioning help, and do you need a purifier?
Switching on the air-conditioner with windows shut is the most convenient way to stay indoors during haze, but cooling a room is not the same as filtering its air.
Tan said conventional home air-conditioners filter larger particles reasonably well, but residents wanting to remove PM2.5 would need a separate purifier.
Syida was more sceptical, calling this one of the biggest misconceptions she hears from clients, friends and family.

“Nearly all home air-conditioning – whether split units or central or ducted units – pulls air from inside the house, cools it, and sends it back into the same room. It isn’t drawing in fresh air from outside and cleaning it on the way,” she said.
Most Malaysian homes use wall-mounted split units, whose mesh filters mainly catch dust, hair and larger debris to protect the equipment rather than clean the air.
“It’s not catching those particles to make your air more breathable. Different job, different solution,” she said.

For those considering a purifier, Syida recommended a genuine high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter, preferably H13, and warned against terms such as “HEPA-type”, “HEPA-like” or “99 per cent HEPA”, which do not necessarily meet a recognised standard.
Tan said buyers should also check the clean air delivery rate (CADR), which indicates how quickly a purifier delivers filtered air, with living areas needing a higher rate than bedrooms.

Syida said a mid-range purifier costing about RM400, with a CADR of 400, had worked effectively in her own 800-square-foot living room, though she described this as personal experience rather than a controlled test.

She said that in a home experiment, indoor PM2.5 readings stayed high despite closed windows and doors, but fell by at least half near the unit within about 10 minutes of switching her purifier to full speed.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Indoor plants are not a substitute for air filtration, and an air quality monitor is the better way to see what is in your home’s air, specialists say. — Pexels pic

Tan said most people would not need to buy a purifier unless they had respiratory problems or other health concerns, though he said households with indoor pets might benefit, as purifiers help clear fur from the air, while animal waste must still be removed quickly before bacteria form.
Syida said there was no need to spend thousands of ringgit on a premium model.
“If you can only afford one, put it in the bedroom. You’re in there seven to eight hours a night breathing the same air while you sleep,” she said.
She advised running the purifier all day on automatic mode if it has a particulate sensor, with windows and doors closed, rather than waiting until the haze visibly worsens.
“By the time you react, the room’s already full of particles and the machine spends the next hour playing catch up,” she said.
What if you can’t afford a purifier?
“If haze has entered your home and you have no filtration and no budget, there’s very little you can do to clean the air,” Syida said.
Wet mopping helps with settled dust but not airborne particles, she said, while ordinary fans do not filter air and may stir up particles that have settled.
Nor should residents count on bowls of water or indoor plants.
“Bowls of water is a weird one — haven’t heard this one before. They do nothing,” Syida said.
On indoor plants, she said: “Effectively no. This is a famous myth that makes the rounds in our industry.”
She said a well-fitted mask could reduce exposure while awake, but fit matters because air leaking around the edges undermines the protection.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
For those who cannot afford a purifier, a well-fitted mask can help reduce exposure to haze particles while awake, but fit matters, an indoor air quality specialist said. — Bernama pic

Syida said ordinary mesh filters are unlikely to clog faster during haze but should still be cleaned as the manufacturer advises, while units with genuine fine-particle filters may need replacing more often.
Tan’s advice suggests many households can manage by limiting outdoor pollution and maintaining good hygiene, while Syida argues that a suitable purifier adds another layer of protection.
For households weighing one, the decision comes down to the occupants’ health needs, the home’s size and layout, outdoor pollution levels and the device’s filtration capacity.
20499cba720fa172: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 26 — With haze conditions continue to affect parts of the country, mental health experts warn that spending prolonged periods indoors can take a toll on mental health and overall wellbeing.

With the haze persisting since early August, many people have become reluctant to engage in outdoor activities, while some have even cancelled social gatherings and cut back on their usual social interactions.

However, these seemingly minor changes, such as avoiding outdoor activities and cancelling social plans, can gradually disrupt people’s daily routines and behaviour, potentially affecting their mood, sleep and overall wellbeing.
Experts, who spoke to Malay Mail, believe that prolonged periods indoors may contribute to frustration, irritability, anxiety, low mood and feelings of isolation.
The toll on mental health

Brian John Dorai, a registered counsellor and senior lecturer in the School of Education, Humanities and Social Sciences at Wawasan Open University, said prolonged haze and indoor confinement can significantly disrupt emotional stability.

“Psychologically, the lack of fresh air and environmental freedom triggers feelings of claustrophobia, irritability, and sometimes even cabin fever, often amplifying anxiety and low mood due to a sense of being trapped, especially for those who dare not open their windows and doors due to anxiety related to the haze,” he said.
He said people may experience behavioural changes when the haze persists for several days or weeks.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Prolonged periods indoors may contribute to frustration, irritability, anxiety, low mood and feelings of isolation. — Picture by Raymond Manuel

“Individuals often exhibit heightened irritability, lethargy, loss of motivation, restlessness, increased screen time, and a tendency to withdraw socially even within the household, when haze persists for weeks,” he said.
Less daylight and exercise can disrupt sleep
Brian also said reduced physical activity, exposure to natural daylight and social interaction could affect sleep and emotional wellbeing.

“Cutting back on physical movement lowers endorphin levels, while reduced natural sunlight disrupts circadian rhythms and vitamin D synthesis, directly impairing sleep architecture, energy levels, and emotional regulation,” he said.
He explained that poor sleep resulting from these disruptions could affect concentration, productivity, mood and the ability to regulate emotions.

“Sleep fragmentation severely compromises executive functions, leading to poor concentration, reduced workplace and academic productivity, heightened emotional reactivity, and a diminished capacity to self-regulate mood,” he said.

Similarly, Universiti Malaya senior medical lecturer and public health medicine specialist Dr Bala Murali Sundram said inadequate or disrupted sleep could impair attention, memory, decision-making and emotional regulation.
“Individuals may become more irritable, less productive and less able to manage everyday stress.

“From an occupational health perspective, poor sleep can also increase fatigue-related errors, reduce work performance and potentially compromise workplace safety, particularly among shift workers and employees performing safety-sensitive tasks,” he said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Thick haze partially obscures the Merdeka Maybank Tower as motorists make their way through Kuala Lumpur on October 16, 2026. — Picture by Raymond Manuel
Poor air quality linked to mental health changes
Dr Bala also pointed to scientific evidence linking poor air quality to changes in mental health.
“Epidemiological studies have found associations between exposure to air pollutants, particularly fine particulate matter (PM2.5), increased the risks of depression and anxiety.
“A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis involving 81 studies reported associations between both short- and long-term air pollution exposure and depression and anxiety.
“Possible biological mechanisms include systemic inflammation, oxidative stress and neuroinflammatory processes affecting the brain,” he said.
PM2.5 refers to microscopic airborne particulate matter with a diameter of 2.5 micrometres or less.
Common sources of PM2.5 include vehicle exhaust, factory emissions, power plant combustion, open waste burning, and dust.
However, Dr Bala said most of the available evidence was observational, meaning a direct cause-and-effect relationship had yet to be established.

He added that the psychological effects of haze were likely caused by a combination of factors, including exposure to air pollution and indirect effects such as reduced physical activity, disrupted routines and social isolation.
Who is most vulnerable during prolonged haze

Dr Bala said several groups were particularly vulnerable to the effects of prolonged haze, with their level of risk influenced not only by their health status but also by their socioeconomic circumstances and access to protective resources.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A man wears face mask as he walks through hazy conditions in Kuala Lumpur on October 17, 2026. — Picture by Raymond Manuel
These groups include:
Children and adolescents: Disruptions to play, schooling, physical activity and social interaction may affect their emotional and behavioural wellbeing.
Older adults: Those with limited mobility or social support may be more susceptible to isolation.
People with existing mental health conditions: Changes in daily routines, sleep patterns and access to support may aggravate their symptoms.
People with chronic respiratory or cardiovascular diseases: Physical symptoms and concerns about their health deteriorating may increase psychological distress.

Outdoor workers and lower-income households: Occupational exposure, limited access to cleaner indoor environments and difficulties in changing working arrangements may contribute to additional stress.
How parents can help children cope with restricted outdoor activities

Experts agreed that suddenly restricting children from participating in outdoor activities could affect their ability to regulate their emotions, as they may struggle to adjust to abrupt changes in their daily routines.

Dr Hilwa Abdullah Mohd Nor, a senior lecturer and clinical psychologist at Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia, said parents play an important role in acknowledging their children’s feelings, maintaining routines and offering alternative ways for them to play, learn and connect with others.
“Children may not always have the language to explain their frustration or disappointment.
“Instead, they may become irritable, clingy, restless or more argumentative.
“Parents should recognise that these behaviours may reflect difficulty adapting to a disrupted routine rather than deliberate misbehaviour,” she said.

Dr Hilwa also suggested that age-appropriate indoor activities, such as drawing, board games, reading, building activities, indoor movement games and creative projects, could help children cope with the restrictions.
“Parents can also maintain children’s social connections through phone or video calls with friends and relatives,” she added.
She said it was also important for parents to explain the haze to their children using simple and reassuring language.
“For example, parents might say that the air outside is unhealthy at the moment, so the family is staying indoors to protect everyone’s health.
“Children should be given opportunities to ask questions without being unnecessarily frightened by the situation,” she said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A notice on the gate of Sekolah Menengah Kebangsaan Subang Bestari announces a school closure due to haze in Shah Alam, Selangor on October 13, 2026. — Picture by Yusof Isa
When to seek professional help
Dr Hilwa said people should not dismiss emotional difficulties as temporary stress if their symptoms become persistent, intense or begin to interfere with their daily lives.

She said professional support from a clinical psychologist or other qualified mental health professional may be necessary when emotional difficulties worsen or affect work, studies, relationships, sleep or daily responsibilities.

Some warning signs include losing interest in activities they previously enjoyed, excessive anxiety, persistent sleep problems, significant behavioural changes or difficulty coping with everyday demands.
She said people with existing mental health conditions should also seek support if their symptoms deteriorate or their usual coping strategies are no longer effective.

“For children and adolescents, parents should seek professional guidance if changes in mood, behaviour, sleep or daily functioning persist or become concerning, rather than waiting for the situation to resolve on its own,” she added.
Dr Hilwa stressed that seeking psychological support should not be viewed as an inability to cope, but as a proactive step towards protecting one’s mental health.
“Just as we take precautions to protect our physical health during haze, we should recognise psychological wellbeing as an equally important part of overall health,” she said.
37507af57f810505: MANNAR (Sri Lanka), Oct 26 — Beneath rotating wind turbines on Sri Lanka’s Mannar peninsula, a fishing net is hauled up the beach by tractor winches and 20 men, but once again the catch is meagre.
“I’ve been fishing here since I was a boy,” said Venkatasamy Kalimuththu, 65, looking disappointedly at the catch — a few good fish, some small fry, and several clumps of seaweed.
“Before the wind turbines were installed, we caught a lot of fish,” he added.
“Now, much less.”

Since they appeared six years ago, the Mannar wind turbines have been blamed for a host of problems — from dwindling catches to floods, fuelling opposition to green energy projects as fuel costs soar.
Local residents are determined to see them dismantled or, at the very least, prevent more from being built.
The opposition comes as war in the Middle East sends fuel and electricity costs soaring, making the shift to renewable energy an economic imperative.
Although he admits he has no proof, Kalimuththu is convinced the spinning blades are driving fish away.
“When the fans rotate, the shadow falls on the water,” he said.
“So the fish don’t swim up to the shallows.”
His colleagues agree, also blaming the turbines — as well as competition from Indian trawlers.
‘Toilets overflow’
“We are not opposed to renewable energy in principle,” said Lesley Jesurajan, a leading figure in the local civil society group OPEnE.
“But not here. There are plenty of other places to install wind turbines.”
Owned by state utility Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB), the turbines line a narrow strip of sand exposed to winds sweeping across the gulf between Sri Lanka and India.
The first phase – 30 turbines with a combined capacity of 104 megawatts – joined the grid in 2020, and construction on another 14 has begun.
A third phase of 52 turbines had been awarded to Indian conglomerate Adani, but the government cancelled the contract in 2025 after a dispute over the price per kilowatt-hour.
Even the first phase has fuelled anger.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

A turbine blade lies near a wind power plant on Sri Lanka’s Mannar peninsula on October 2. The government has frozen new projects in Mannar to ease local opposition, as residents blame the turbines for dwindling catches and floods. — AFP pic
Benedict Mary Vijiliya’s village, around 100 metres (330 feet) from the coast, is surrounded by wind turbines.
She claims concrete foundations and trenches for access roads have prevented rainwater from draining towards the sea.

“During the monsoon rains, the water comes up to our waists and the toilets overflow,” complains Vijiliya, president of the Women’s Rural Development Society (WRDS), showing photographs on her phone of her home submerged under about a metre of water.
“We never had experienced that before 2020. Our homes are damaged, our cattle and our crops are affected, our livelihood is impacted and we can’t even drink the water of our well anymore.”
‘Cheating people’
In neighbouring Pesalai, fishing incomes have plummeted, said A. Stanislas Peries, head of the local fishermen’s cooperative.
“Before, people could earn up to 5,000 rupees (US$15, RM61) a day from fishing. Now they barely make more than 1,000 (RM12). Things have become very difficult.”
Energy Minister Anura Karunathilaka said he had heard the complaints.
“We are carrying out feasibility studies,” he said.
“Once we implement this...the flood situation they are currently facing can be reduced.”
The government aims to generate 70 per cent of the country’s electricity from renewable sources by 2030, including wind power.
But it has frozen new projects in Mannar to ease local opposition.
“We have already pledged... that only those projects already approved will be carried out.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

A fisherman carries nets along a beach near a wind power plant on Sri Lanka’s Mannar peninsula on October 3. The government aims to generate 70 per cent of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030 but has frozen new projects in Mannar to ease local opposition. — AFP pic
Father S. Marcus, a Catholic priest and head of the Mannar Citizens’ Committee, remains unconvinced.
“They had several times promised mitigation measures but nothing happened ... they are cheating our people,” he added.
At his initiative, residents have filed two complaints in Sri Lankan courts.
But a separate one has been filed against him.
“Apparently, we are disrupting the government,” he said.
“But we will not back down — we will put an end to all this.” — AFP
ab330fcdfb6c96fa: WASHINGTON, Oct 26 — Companies and government agencies rushed this week to patch two critical flaws in PHP, the programming language that runs a large share of the world’s websites.
The vulnerability to potential hackers was found by using a powerful model from OpenAI in one of the most high-profile demonstrations of AI’s cyber capabilities.

AFP spoke with Michael Daniel, president of the Cyber Threat Alliance and a former White House cybersecurity coordinator under former US president Barack Obama, about what the episode means as AI tools find software flaws faster than ever.
The interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Q: What does the PHP episode tell us?

A: This is the beginning of a pretty chaotic period, given the abilities of the advanced models. I’ve been saying for years that the logical conclusion of these AI models being able to find vulnerabilities at speed and at scale is that there’s going to be a flood of these vulnerabilities.
Rob Joyce [former cybersecurity director at the US National Security Agency] has referred to it as the great cleansing forest fire of old software. I’ve talked about our tech debt coming due.

The incentives have been for people to keep software as long as possible, and we don’t really factor these risks into the cost of having the software. You’re not incurring a direct cost on your books for this old software, but in reality you are, only it’s an implicit cost until something like this happens.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Former White House cybersecurity coordinator Michael Daniel who now heads Cyber Threat Alliance, a non-profit that facilitates threat intelligence sharing among cybersecurity firms, says the PHP patch scramble is just the start of a flood of AI-found bugs. — Anadolu pic via AFP
Q: What should organizations be doing?
A: Preparing to get your software updated, be prepared to keep it updated, and be prepared to implement patches when they come out.
There’s going to be a flood of vulnerabilities, a flood of patches and a flood of mitigations, and not all of them will be created equal.
For a lot of smaller organizations that don’t have a lot of internal capacity, what you’ve got to do is shift your organization to be able to accept the vendor updates as fast as you can.
Q: Is every flaw dangerous?

A: Historically, the exploitation rate for vulnerabilities has been five or six percent, and there’s no indication that number is going up. But now when bad guys exploit a vulnerability, they’re able to do so much more quickly.
It used to take a month or two for a proof of concept to come out, and then another month or two for it to show up in exploit kits (used by bad actors). That’s now measured in hours or days.
Q: What does that mean for large companies?
A: Most businesses essentially ran a zero-risk tolerance for breaking things, so they would test the hell out of a patch before they put it into production. Now they don’t have that time.
If the risk of breaking something by putting this patch into place is one percent, but the risk of being attacked could cost me 50 million dollars…now I’ve got an interesting trade-off.
Q: Are advanced AI tools reliable at finding real flaws?

A: There’s a lot of noise. The PHP one is a prime example of a real one, but there’s an awful lot out there that are either not real or are on software that’s never exposed to the internet. We’ve got to improve our triage system.
Q: Where does this lead us in two or three years?

A: We’re going to turn these AI tools on software that hasn’t been deployed yet, so one would hope we start to deploy software that has fewer vulnerabilities to begin with. You burn out all the old stuff, and it makes way for new growth that’s more secure from the beginning.
It’s not like this solves our cybersecurity problem, but it does change the nature of it going forward. — AFP

aa872cb60c5482a3: KUALA LUMPUR: They came with different stories and different ways of seeing the world. But through their paintings, six artists shared a hope - to make life a little easier for someone else.

That hope found a generous response at "Art4Good: Painting from the Heart", which raised RM536,000 in gross proceeds for the Free Food Society (FFS) and the Society for the Severely Mentally Handicapped (SSMH).
With FMT as its media partner, the exhibition ran from Oct 14 to 18 at Bangsar Shopping Centre, with a total of 88 paintings sold. It surpassed its RM400,000 fundraising target.
That generosity will help FFS continue providing food aid to 85 B40 families in Desa Rejang, Setapak, and tuition for more than 100 primary and secondary schoolchildren.

At SSMH’s centre in Sea Park, Petaling Jaya, the funds will support specialised therapy and individual training to help children with severe disabilities develop everyday skills and reach their full potential.
Helping make this possible were artists who gave months of their time and talent, alongside buyers, bidders, sponsors, volunteers and other supporters.
Among the most heartening achievements was that of the exhibition’s youngest artist, eight-year-old Winsen Loke, who sold 26 artworks.
Winsen, who has global developmental delay and mild cerebral palsy, creates paintings by tapping his wrist and palm against paper or canvas.
He attends SSMH, where rehabilitative therapy has helped him develop better balance and sit upright for about 15 minutes without falling over.
At the exhibition launch, his mother, Tan Boon See, spoke of the possibilities she hopes others will recognise in children like him.
“Everyone is unique. Every child, even a handicapped one, has potential. So don’t give up on them,” she said.

Fellow artist Yoon Chooi Wan saw all eight of her Chinese brush paintings find buyers. Tan Ken Ming, who has Asperger’s syndrome, sold three of his seven artworks, while Oon Soon Keat sold one of four paintings.
Principal artist Yeow Teck Chai sold 50 paintings and continued receiving orders after the exhibition ended.
Former international trade and industry minister Rafidah Aziz, who launched the exhibition, also contributed eight paintings to a silent auction that raised RM83,600.
She welcomed the chance to support the charities through her art, crediting the sponsors, volunteers, media and wider community who helped turn the paintings into practical help for those in need.
“I am happy that the silent auction of my paintings contributed towards helping the charities,” she said.

For Yeow, the exhibition was a satisfying end to months of preparation for his fourth charity showcase. He had been painting daily since late last year, enjoying the creative process as much as the knowledge that each piece could help someone else.
“I am tired I feel happy that the entire team worked really hard to make this event a success,” said the former deputy director-general of the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (Mida).

SSMH president Fadillah Yakin said the funds would go a long way towards sustaining its work with the children and their families. For FFS president Ali Abdul Kadir, it meant being able to continue providing food aid and tuition to families who need that support.

For the two charities, the paintings hold the promise of more ordinary, precious moments: a family having enough to eat, a student finding their way through a difficult lesson, or a parent watching their child master a new skill such as learning to sit a little steadier.

199521dac74e9d77: Pada 22 Okt lalu, Pengerusi BN Zahid Hamidi beritahu media gabungan yang dipimpinnya akan mengumumkan calon PRN Melaka bersama dengan PAS dan rakan strategiknya pada Sabtu 24 Okt.
