Keesokan harinya iaitu 23 Okt tampil Timbalan Presiden PAS Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man menafikan partinya akan umum calon PRN Melaka mereka atas pentas yang sama dengan BN dan pada Sabtu yang dikatan Zahid.

Kata Tuan Ibrhim PAS akan umum pada minggu minggu akhir -sama ada 28 atau 29 Okt. Kata Pengerusi BN Melaka Ab Rauf Yusoh ini hanyalah isu teknikal berkaitan status Perikatan Nasional (PN) di mahkamah. Bagi saya ini hanya bikin gempak. So don’t read too much into it.

Maka pada Sabtu lalu BN mengumumkanlah calon PRN Melaka mereka bersendrian bukan bersama PAS. Dan Zahid mengumumkan BN akan letak calon pada 21 kerusi DUN Melaka. Baki tujuh diperuntuk kepada PAS dan rakan strategiknya.

Namun semasa Zahid membuat pengumuman, Presiden MCA Wee Ka Siong dan pasukannya keluar dewan (tempat pengumuman dibuat) tanda protes. MCA tak puas hati cuma diberi dua kerusi untuk ditandingi. Wee dakwa pengagihan kerusi dibuat tanpa perbicangan menyeluruh dengan partinya.

Bagi saya ini sekadar drama. Keluar dewan bukan bererti MCA keluar BN. Bukan boikot PRN Melaka. Kata seorang ahli kumpulan sembang WhatsApp yang saya turut menganggotai: “Wayang only - later they will wink and hug each other”.
Apa pun MCA memang ada sebab dan alasan untuk rasa tidak puas hati seperti dihuraikan Ketua Penyelidik Ilham Centre Yusri Ibrahim menerusi hantaran di Facebook. Ini kita cerita sebentar lagi.

Kata Zahid kerjasama BN dengan PAS di Melaka mampu membawa mereka selangkah lebih dekat ke Putrajaya jika membuahkan hasil yang baik. Lalu beliau menyeru PAS dan BN mengetepikan permusuhan lama untuk saling membantu.

“Insya-Allah jika keserasian ini dapat kita jalankan terowong ke Putrajaya akan lebih cerah,” katanya pada majlis pengumuman calon PRN Melaka malam Sabtu lalu. Jelas Zahid mahu apa yang dipanggil ‘gelombang biru’ diteruskan ke Melaka setelah melanda Johor dan Negeri Sembilan.
Apa yang dipanggil ‘gelombang hijau’ yang tercetus pada PRU15 pada 2022 dan diikuti beberapa pilihan raya negeri tahun berikutnya sudah dinamakan ‘gelombang biru”.
Ini berikutan kemenangan BN di PRN Johor dan Negeri Sembilan tahun ini . Tetapi perlu diingat ia diperolehi dengan kerjasama PAS.
Di PRN Johor PAS bertanding 11 kerusi. Di Negeri Sembilan lima. Presiden PAS Hadi Awang mengarahkan penyokong partinya mengundi calon BN dl kawasanPAS tidak bertanding .
Saya ulang apa yang saya pernah katakan pada beberapa penulisan sebelum ini bahawa kerjasaam BN (baca Umno) dengan PAS berjaya kerana PAS yang banyak beralah.

They were willing to have peanuts as long as the electoral pact would bring success. And indeed it brought success. PAS is no angel. Mereka lakukan ini semua kerana political survival berdasarkan political reality yakni PAS tidak boleh menang di Johor dan Negeri Sembilan on its own.
Sekarang PAS dikehendaki menerima hanya tujuh kerusi di Melaka untuk diagihkan antara mereka, Wawasan, Gerakan, MIPP dan Pejuang. Secara rambang PAS got the short end of the bargain. Again.

Tetapi mereka akan terima tawaran itu.Sekali lagi PAS yang ‘mengalah’. Berkorban demi kemenangan BN-PAS. Tentunya kerana ada big picture . Persoalan yang selalu saya bangitkan – sampai bila ia akan beralah ?
Adakah PAS akan puas hati dengan hanya makan kacang apabila PRU16 diadakan? Bagaimana pula di Kelantan dan Terenggnau dua kubu kuat mereka. Begitu juga di Kedah dan Perlis.
Adakah PAS akan beri dengan senyum manis banyak kerusi kepada Umno? Apa lagi realiti di kedua negeri itu-Umno tak akan menang bersendirian.
Berbalik kepada protes MCA yang disebut tadi. Menurut Yusri, diberi hanya dua kerusi MCA mungkin rasa ini akan membantutkan momentum sokongan terhadap mereka.

Ini berpandu prestasi baik di Negeri Sembilan dan Johor. Tetapi bagi saya MCA lupa prestasi baik itu terjalin kerana PAS meminta penyokongnya – orang Melayu islam–mengundi calon MCA berdasarkan eletroral pact PAS - BN.

Kata Yusri jumlah calon etnik Cina mewakili BN tidak selari dengan komposisi etnik pengundi Melaka. Dibenarkan bertanding hanya dua kerusi iaitu hanya 7% daripada keseluruhan 28 kerusi. Atau hanya 9% daripada 21 kerusi yang ditandingi BN. Maka dianggap kecil dan tidak munasabah oleh MCA.
Apa lagi lawan utama mereka iaitu DAP diberi sehingga tujuh kerusi oleh Pakatan Harapan (PH) untuk ditandingi. Bahkan PKR juga menamakan calon etnik Cina mereka.

Dan kata Yusri MCA mungkin merasakan peluang untuk menang di kawasan yang disandang DAP lebih besar jika mereka mereka yang bertanding berbanding calon PAS (diwakili calon Dewan Himpunan Pendukung PAS) atau Gerakan.

Yang paling menarik bagi saya ialah apabila Yusri berkata MCA mungkin bertanya Umno yang bersemangat dengan agenda penyatuan ummah dengan PAS tetapi mengapa tidak beri kerusi mereka (Umno) kepada PAS? Sebaliknya beri kerusi tradisi MCA kepada PAS.
Bagi saya hanya satu kesimpulan- let the fight begin.

eb58e7e8a5694b2b: As the term “middle powers” has gained currency this year, it has forced us to ask which countries actually belong to this grouping. After all, shouldn’t most states be described that way?
With his much-cited speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney revived a debate about shifting power structures in today’s world.
He believes we are seeing a “rupture” in the global order, one that will require middle powers to cooperate to resist economic coercion and political domination by others.
Although he did not mention the US, President Donald Trump immediately sensed, correctly, that some of Carney’s remarks were directed against him.
But, again, how should the middle powers that Carney had in mind be distinguished from the other powers of our time, if at all? Perhaps one should start by discussing those other powers.

It was some time ago that “superpower” was applied to nation-states that wielded powers well beyond any others on the global stage. After World War II, this term was used to describe not only the US and the Soviet Union, but also, for a very short period, the British Empire.

In the decades that followed, the two unquestioned superpowers were defined by their massive nuclear arsenals—with each commanding tens of thousands of warheads—and their ability to deliver them anywhere in the world in a matter of minutes, with no possibility to defend against an attack. Each had the power to annihilate the other within a half-hour.

Over time, other states acquired nuclear weapons, but none had the capacity or the will to develop arsenals that would put them on the same level as the two superpowers. Then came the collapse of the Soviet Union, after which the term superpower started to fall out of use.

The US was occasionally still described as such, but during this brief “unipolar era,” it was also bestowed with a new term: Hubert Védrine, France’s foreign minister between 1997 and 2002, called it a hyperpuissance.

Today, the US remains very powerful, and Russia still commands huge military resources, including the world’s largest nuclear arsenal. Yet both countries’ powers have increasingly come to be defined by their obvious limitations.

Despite having mobilised its vast conventional arsenal, Russia has not been able to subjugate its substantially smaller neighbour, Ukraine. And despite Trump constantly boasting about his country’s military might, his war on Iran has so far yielded little more than higher oil prices and a destabilising stalemate.

The failure to achieve victory in their respective wars of choice demonstrates that the US and Russia no longer qualify as “superpowers”. Are they even great powers, or do they ultimately belong to the same, broad category of middle powers?

Whatever the case, the age of superpowers is over. Even the most nominally powerful countries are highly constrained. The limits of their powers have been laid bare, regardless of whether they realise it yet.

Though middle powers come in many different shapes and sizes, most are at least aware of their status. Neither India nor Brazil nor Canada can use military power to shape its political environment to its liking.

Instead, each must rely on economic engagement and political relationship-building to exert influence. But the same applies to the US, Russia, and other larger, more powerful players like the European Union.
The late Joseph Nye still has much to teach today’s middle powers. He famously introduced the concept of “soft power” to draw a distinction between persuasion and coercion in international relations.

While military capability confers “hard power,” soft power—what Nye termed “the power of attraction”—comes from cultural exports, economic ties, diplomacy, goodwill, and trust built up over many years. Perhaps the world’s middle powers can be defined along these lines, namely as those who must rely primarily on soft power.

Of course, some countries will still harbour visions of grandeur, having convinced themselves that hard power is enough to bend others to their will. It might take some time for recognition of their reduced status to sink in. But whatever those in Moscow or Washington tell themselves, the fact is that the world has changed. There are no superpowers any longer.
Carl Bildt is a former prime minister and foreign minister of Sweden.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

61af4596c875979f: PRAGUE: Several thousand people gathered in Prague on Sunday to protest against plans to change the funding system for public television and radio, accusing the government of stifling press freedom.
The Czech lower house of parliament voted on Saturday to fast-track a bill that would abolish licence fees for public media and replace them with direct allocations from the state budget.
The legislation, backed by the governing coalition led by Prime Minister Andrej Babis and including two far-right parties, must still be passed by the upper house before becoming law.
The plans have drawn criticism from the opposition, which has pledged to challenge them in the constitutional court.
In Prague's Old Town Square, protester Petr Cekal, a 26-year-old architecture student, said politicians "want to restrict press freedom", which he finds "quite alarming".
Milan Kotal, 94, said that "in my lifetime there have already been two state takeovers of our television in Prague: once by the Nazis during the war and then by the Communists until 1989.
"Today the government is allowing itself things we cannot accept," he said.
Under the proposed reform, state television and radio would see their budgets cut by around 15%.
The coalition argues that both public broadcasters need to make savings and insists that changing their funding model will have no impact on editorial independence or programme content.
"No one wants to interfere with programming or news coverage," Babis wrote on X on Saturday.
"The funds will be guaranteed directly by law as a mandatory expenditure, so no government will be able to arbitrarily cut them based on whether it likes the broadcasting or not," he said.
The European Broadcasting Union, European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders and the International Press Institute are among the organisations that have criticised the plans.
"The very future of the country for the coming decades is at stake. The government is testing how far it can go," protest organisers said in their call to demonstrate.
A larger demonstration is planned in Prague on Nov 15.
President Petr Pavel, who has often clashed with Babis since he returned to power in 2025, said he believed that "public service media are among the fundamental pillars of our democracy".
"Hasty steps that cannot be reversed cannot be taken," he wrote on X.
Trust in the media is low in the Czech Republic at around 30–33 percent, according to the Reuters Institute Digital News Report 2026.
"Public service broadcasters remain the most trusted brands, despite increasing attempts by various political actors to undermine their credibility," the report said.

6cdee2a32a0fd3c6: AUSTIN: Kimi Antonelli moved to within striking distance of his first world championship title as he powered to an emphatic victory at the US Grand Prix in Austin on Sunday.

It was his ninth win of the season and with his only rivals Mercedes teammate George Russell and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton finishing eighth and fourth respectively, the 20-year-old Italian needs just to come in ninth in next week's race in Mexico to become the youngest ever Formula One champion.
He is also set to become the first Italian to win the title since Alberto Ascari in 1953.
Antonelli finished over 13 seconds ahead of the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc with Red Bull's Max Verstappen completing the podium.

Antonelli started the race in pole position and after a clean start already had a 2sec lead by the end of the opening lap, at which point the result never seemed in doubt, mechanical failure and pit stop disasters notwithstanding.

Verstappen was beaten off the start by Leclerc, who started in third, but the four-time world champion wasted no time in reclaiming second spot. Leclerc, however, overtook him in the latter part of the race and Verstappen was left hanging on for third as Hamilton also closed.

Antonelli would have become the youngest ever champion, smashing the current record of Sebastian Vettel who was 23 years and 133 days when he won his fist title in 2010, if Russell had finished lower than eighth and Hamilton failed to make the top four.
Russell, who has had some terrible luck all season, was hit with a 5sec penalty for running off the track on the opening lap and struggled to get past McLaren's Oscar Piastri who came in seventh.
Lando Norris, the outgoing champion, was running second until the closing laps when his tyres appeared to give up and he had to settle for fifth with Isack Hadjar sixth in the second Red Bull.

40333d012dcd666d: BARCELONA: Kylian Mbappe struck twice to earn Jose Mourinho's Real Madrid a 2-1 Clasico victory over LaLiga leaders Barcelona on Sunday at Camp Nou, cutting the gap to three points.

Barca defender Pau Cubarsi twice reacted well to shut down Mbappe, while Real Madrid's Marc Cucurella took a rapid liking for Lamine Yamal's shirt, constantly grabbing at the 19-year-old winger.
Anthony Gordon, playing in his first Clasico since joining Barcelona from Newcastle, backheeled the ball to Raphinha, who fired narrowly wide as Barca threatened.

Sting in the tail

There was a sting in the tail for the Catalans though as substitute Gabriel Jesus lost possession and Madrid raced through on goal.
Eduardo Camavinga beat Cubarsi and unselfishly cut the ball back for Mbappe to tuck home his second of the night into an empty net with Joan Garcia drawn out of position.

651cd257d491a92a: RIO DE JANEIRO: Brazil's Supreme Court extended voting time for two hours on Sunday, generating chaos in a knife-edge election race Sunday between right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro and leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.

Lula, 80, was first to ask the courts to extend voting, claiming buses had been pulled from circulation in Sao Paulo and key northeastern cities, a bastion of his support, claiming "something abominable is happening".
A Supreme Court ruling just minutes after polls were set to close at 5pm local time, ordered voting extended across the country until 7pm, citing the "seriousness of the facts narrated".
Lula is facing stiff competition from Flavio Bolsonaro, who stunned the left by winning the most votes in a first-round election three week ago.
Final polls showed the pair neck-and-neck in Sunday's runoff.
Lula said that 40% of buses were pulled from service in Sao Paulo, a problem also seen in several cities in northeastern Brazil, where he held a commanding lead in the first round.
A regional electoral court ordered the arrest of Salvador's transport secretary for failing to offer free transport on election day.

Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, also asked for an extension due to heavy rains in the south and southeast of Brazil -- where much of his support is concentrated.

Brazil uses electronic voting machines -- and results are typically available in a few hours after polls close. Some tallies had already started streaming in when polling stations where ordered to stay open.
In a clarification, Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin said the order only applied to "locations where polling stations have not yet been closed."
'We are watching'
Sunday's runoff will determine whether Brazil remains one of Latin America's few leftist nations or joins a regional swing to the right championed by US President Donald Trump.
Lula, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, has pitched himself as a bulwark against US interference and democratic backsliding.
Trump, an ally of Flavio Bolsonaro's father, simply said "we are watching, yeah," when asked about Brazil's election on Sunday.
The 45-year-old senator has vowed to crack down on crime and slash government spending, while handing Brazil to "the Lord Jesus Christ."
"The time has come for real change," he declared after voting in Rio de Janeiro.

"This is about renewal, enough of the same old thing," 67-year-old retiree Eduardo Viana told AFP, adding that Lula "says he governs for the poor...just look, people can't even go to the supermarket."
Bolsonaro presents himself as more moderate than his firebrand father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after he lost in the 2022 elections.

After its first-round defeat, the left swung into action with massive rallies highlighting Jair Bolsonaro's chaotic handling of the Covid pandemic, devastation of the Amazon rainforest and cuts to public programs.
Deforestation of the world's largest rainforest has hit its lowest level in four decades under Lula.
Yet, as the El Nino weather phenomenon fueled fires across the Amazon in recent weeks, and rains lashed the south, climate change barely featured in the campaign.
Lula's revamp
Lula, revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, made a dramatic comeback to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months.
The charges, annulled on procedural grounds, have continued to haunt him.
In his third term he has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but voters complain about the cost of living and a sense of insecurity.

The bitterly divisive campaign alienated many voters, including doorman Joao Inacio Oliveira, who told AFP he would make a last-minute decision at the polling station.

4b22ee1f7844c295: Being Mozambican is a matter of belonging — regardless of one’s origin, appearance, or surname
Originally published on Global Voices
Indians in Mozambique celebrating the Hindu festival of Navratri. Image by Kash_if via Flickr. CC BY 2.0.

In Mozambique, the word monhé has a much deeper history than its everyday use might suggest. Depending on who says it and the context, it can simply be a reference to the population of Indian origin, an identity marker, or a prejudiced remark. But behind the word there is a history of migration, trade, colonialism, independence, displacement, and, above all, belonging.

The question of who is Mozambican gets particularly interesting when we look at the communities of Indian origin, who have lived in the country for several generations. Are they Mozambicans? Indians? Foreigners? Or, in some cases, stateless persons? The answer cannot be found in appearance, surname, religion, or family origin alone. It is found in the country’s history and, particularly, in its nationality law.
A presence older than modern borders

The presence of people originating from the Indian subcontinent in the lands we now call Mozambique predates the country’s independence and, in many instances, predates the demarcation of the current political borders. The Indian Ocean’s trade networks connected the East African coast to South Asia long before 1975, the year Mozambique gained its independence. Over time, merchants, families, and whole communities settled in different parts of the country.

During the Portuguese colonial period, this took place within a political structure that gave people nationalities and legal statuses according to the rules of the empire. As such, “being of Indian origin” never meant automatically “being an Indian citizen.” A person can have Indian ancestry and at the same time hold Portuguese, Indian, Pakistani, or any other nationality, which could leave people in a complex bureaucratic situation. This distinction became especially important when the empire came to an end.
1975: When the question “Whose country is this?” took on a new meaning

Mozambique’s independence, made official on June 25th, 1975, did not just mean a transfer of political power. It also implied the need to define who would legally receive the new state, which was known as the New State. The Nationality Law of 1975 was key to answering that question. Among its provisions were rules that recognized as Mozambicans certain people born in the territory and resident in Mozambique at the time of independence, as well as other criteria related to birth, family links, and residence. The legislation would thus transform a heterogeneous imperial population into a national political community.

For many families of Indian origin who lived in Mozambique for decades or generations, this transformation would mean a fundamental change: no longer being legally associated with a colonial power or a foreign nationality and becoming part of the new Mozambican nation. But the experience of this transition was not the same for everybody.
When identity doesn’t fit neatly into a passport

Decolonization created situations where identity, origin, and nationality did not match. Imagine a family history across three generations: the grandparents born in India, the parents born in Mozambique during the colonial period, and the children born after independence. Which nationality should each generation have? The answer may depend on specific legal circumstances: place of birth, the parents’ nationality, residence in Mozambique at its independence, existing documentation, and any decisions to opt for or relinquish nationality.

Here, the issue of statelessness arises. A stateless person is somebody who is not considered a national by any state’s legislation. It is not an ambiguous cultural identity or feeling divided between two countries, but a legal status.

After decolonization, some people in former colonial territories, such as Angola and Mozambique, faced this problem: some were no longer recognized as nationals by the former colonial power without any other nationalities automatically being granted. This does not mean, though, that the whole Indian community in Mozambique became stateless. This generalization would be historically and legally incorrect.
“Monhé” is not a nationality

This may be where everyday language misleads us. The term “Monhé” may be used as an identity category, but it is not a legal category. Somebody called a monhé can be as Mozambican as anybody else born or naturalized in the country. They may have been born in Maputo, Nampula, Beira, or Quelimane, speak Portuguese or another Mozambican language, have had family in Mozambique for several generations, and never have lived in India. Your ancestry does not disqualify your citizenship.

Likewise, a person of Indian origin living in Mozambique can be a citizen of another country. And, in certain cases, they may have difficulties in proving or acquiring a nationality. As such, it is important to distinguish three concepts that are often confused: origin, nationality, and citizenship. A person’s origin may be Indian. Their identity can be simultaneously Mozambican and Indian. Nationality, though, is a legal relationship between an individual and a state.
A community across oceans
The history of so-called monhés in Mozambican identity also challenges an overly simplistic view of nationality.

Mozambique has always been a space where people cross paths. Africans, Arabs, Indians, Portuguese, and other peoples participated, at different moments, in the country’s social, economic, and cultural development. The Mozambican coast, in particular, cannot be understood without movements across the Indian Ocean.

This is why it may be inappropriate to think of the Indian diaspora as forever an “outsider” population. For many of these families, Mozambique is not simply the country where they live. It is the country where they were born, where their parents were born, where their ancestors are buried, and where they built their lives. India may be their family origin. Mozambique is, for many, a homeland.
The ongoing question

Around half a century after independence, the question of nationality continues to be more than a matter of just documents. It is a question of recognition. Who has the right to say “I am Mozambican”? Is it enough to have been born in the country? Have Mozambican parents? Have lived in the country for decades? Participate in society? Speak its languages? Share a collective memory? Or will some people continue to be seen as foreigners by many, despite legally being citizens? It is in this space between the law and general perception that many identities exist.

This evokes the concept of a “bridge” — Mozambique’s Indian-origin community historically finds itself between different spaces: Africa and Asia, family tradition and national identity, migratory memory and territorial belonging. But being between two shores does not necessarily mean not belonging to either. Sometimes it means belonging to both. And, for some, it means discovering that their family history crossed oceans long before modern passports decided which country a person belonged to.

The history of Mozambique’s monhés is thus also a history about the very meaning of being Mozambican. Not a story of people who simply “came from outside,” but a story of people who, over generations, helped build the country, while continuing to negotiate, within their families and wider society the fundamental question that follows all those who migrate: where, in the end, is home?

003a6a0d932a932b: I think a lot about time. How we consume it, save it, enjoy it, spend it. How it can be interminably slow or rush by before you know it.

Our language subtly instructs us about our concept of time: We are urged to “savor the moment”; we want to “be present.” Even store clerks bid us to “have a good day”, as if you control whether this 24-hour period will be good or not. You can, of course, try your best to have a good day, and sometimes succeed – unless the universe has other plans for you.1
I’ve always been fascinated by time; maybe that’s why I was so intrigued by watches as a kid. A few recent events have me thinking about time more than usual: a big birthday, a loss, other events …
Age

I never had a midlife crisis. Perhaps it was too cliché. Big round birthdays and aging never bothered me. The only experience I had relative to age was waking up on the morning of my 60th birthday and immediately thinking, “Start of the fourth quarter, down by 7 – you’re still in this thing, but lots to do. Get busy!”

The result was a new book, some personal projects, financial and estate planning, and less procrastination on major purchases, travel, and activities I had been putting off for no good reason. As an immortal, I would get around to them eventually. Once the 19-year-old in me admitted immortality was no longer operative, I suddenly felt an urgency to check off some boxes. No, not a bucket list, just a short inventory of unfulfilled desires I suddenly felt the urge to make happen.
Hey, wait a second…
Impermanence
Our house developed an exterior leak that dripped into the basement. To prep for the contractors, we cleared out a lot of accumulated junk. The big surprise: 6 MacBooks dating back to the 2000s.

Six! Each one was a thing: expensive, useful, important, yet oh so temporary. We were warned: “Don’t throw away old laptops unless you removed the hard drives!” Looking at these old, battered MacBooks, I remember the excitement of buying them: Faster, better, improved! When we buy something new, we forget it will eventually wear out, get damaged, become less useful, get replaced or discarded. Everything!
The second law of thermodynamics is a bitch.
Illusion

Here’s something you might not have considered: Time, at least as an objective concept outside human consciousness, doesn’t exist. It’s (mostly) a human creation; no chrono particles, no celestial timekeeper, no physical mechanism governs time’s passage. Our experience is an illusion, a function of our sensory inputs colliding with our consciousness…

Physics recognizes Time is a useful construct, a handy artifice for comparing forces relative to one another. “T” in equations is time as a dimension between other vectors. You use it to measure speed or distance, but mostly relative to each other. Every measure of time seems to quantify only an object’s motion, whether it’s the vibration of a Cesium atom or the hands on a clock.2

I wonder: Does Time exist independently of us, conscious beings? Without us, does the relative motion of objects in 3-dimensional space include time – or is that simply a convenient human assumption? 3

The flow of time seems especially illusory: The sense of RIGHT HERE AND NOW, the intersection of THIS instant (T) and THIS location (X, Y, & Z), is moving forward, a present “now” that advances tick by tick, second by second, and millennia by millennia. I struggle to believe this is anything other than the human mind trying to make sense of the experiential universe…
Our experience of Time, which changes so radically over our lives, is an illusion.
Money is Time
I contributed a chapter to the new book “How I Invest My Money Volume Two,” which was published this week.
Excellent financial advice needs specific personalization; I wanted to write something universal. My chapter, titled “Money Is Time,” is a tight 860 words, but has three concepts worth sharing:
First, Money is society’s measure of the economic contributions you make with your time (including effort, expertise, insight, skill, etc., which are themselves functions of time).

Second, we all get precisely 24 hours a day. Each of us is born wealthy in time, with endless, infinite hours, days, weeks, months, and years, which we fritter away when young. Later in life, we learn that time is our stock in trade.

And third, Money IS Time. Every purchase you make is an investment of your insultingly limited time. The days may be long, but the decades are short. Keep this front of mind as you spend your finite supply of time.
Time Travel
As a sci-fi fan, I’ve sat through more than my fair share of time-travel flicks. Screenwriters and novelists seem to ignore two issues.

The first is Location: When you travel back in time, the planet you’re standing on will have moved – millions or billions of miles away. The Earth orbits the Sun at 66,600 mph; the Sun makes a 260-million-year route around the Milky Way at 515,000 mph; even the Earth’s rotation is 1,040 mph. You must surmise your position relative to the galactic expansion at 515,000 mph, despite its occasional changes in acceleration. 4

In total, we are moving at 828,000 mph. Time travel for a century, and you space travel 725 billion miles (best of luck calculating that precisely). Off by a trillionth of a %, e.g., ~three-quarters of a mile, you materialize inside Earth’s crust (deadly) or nearly 4,000 feet in the air before gravity ends you. Greater errors deliver you into the vacuum of space.

My second issue is the Arrow of Time. It annoys me to send people into a nondeterministic future that hasn’t happened yet. I don’t buy the thesis of a Universe as a block of past, present, and future all occurring at once – it lacks causality.5

In my version of time travel, you can go into the past, but only to return to the point from which you departed. But you cannot visit the Restaurant at the End of the Universe because it hasn’t happened yet. Between now and then, many things will shape what actually happens. But until then, the future doesn’t exist.6
Dog Time

People often think of their lives in terms of blocks of time: You lived in this house or apartment; you worked at this job or that one; you dated or married this person. These blocks make up the eras of your life.

I sometimes think of my life in terms of dogs: Erev was a Labrador retriever I had as a kid; Killer was the stray I adopted in college (and my dad fell in love with); when we moved out of the city, we rescued Max, a shepherd-bearded mutt puppy; Jackson was a Labradoodle who kept Max young until he was 17. Lexi (died young of encephalitis), then Kodie (who is 5), followed Jack. Teddy, a Portuguese Water Dog, followed Max. We had to say goodbye to him last week, and even though I knew it was coming, the grief still shocked me.

Dogs gauge time by how your scent slowly fades since you left the house. If you return at the ~same time every day, they approximate that by how your scent declines over the day. They know when you are returning by that marker.

We all lose friends and family; our relationships are complicated, filled with joy, angst, baggage, walls, and emotions. None of that complexity exists with dogs – they are pure, unconditional love; when they depart, the wound finds you naked and defenseless…
Optionality

As you get older, you begin to realize you kinda know how the movie ends: what you’ve accomplished, what you’ve earned, the people you affected, and who affected you. Not a full accounting, but a modest recognition of who you have become.

It begins to set: You realize what is increasingly unlikely to occur. Projects that might take 5, 10, or 20 years to reach fruition, learning a new language, starting a business, learning to read music, seem difficult to impossible.
That is the biggest disillusionment about aging: What you gain in agency, you lose in optionality.
1. Classic Yiddish expression: “Man plans, and God laughs…”

2. To be precise: One second is officially defined as “the duration of exactly 9,192,631,770 periods of radiation corresponding to the transition between the two hyperfine levels of the ground state of a Cesium-133 atom.”
So, not really a thing on its own; if something only exists relative to an actual thing’s motion, does it really exist at all?

3. Einstein would argue that Relativity treats spacetime as a geometric object with four dimensions – X, Y, Z, and T. That distinction is probably the closest thing to Time as an objective entity independent of us, as anything else in physics.
I’m not sure how persuasive that is to me. Also, attempts to quantize gravity, such as the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, has no T. Time vanishes from the equations entirely

4. Best current estimates are that the expansion rate, the Hubble parameter H(t), was falling for the first 8ish billion years after the Big Bang. Then around 5ish billion years ago, the expansion diluted matter enough to allow dark energy to take over – and the expansion of the universe began accelerating. It’s an adequate Nobel Prize-winning theory, at least until a better one comes along.
5. Alternative timelines will resolve the grandfather (or any other) paradox, but do not explain where a new universe of matter and energy came from.
6. At least, in the universe I inhabit…

df70790ae9e76c4e: SEOUL, Oct 25 — The latest instalment of the Call of Duty video game franchise, featuring a full-scale North Korean invasion of South Korea, has topped sales charts in the would-be target, even as real-life border tensions are ratcheting higher.
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, the latest edition of the globally popular franchise, is set against a backdrop of tensions between the United States and Russia.
Its Friday release comes on the heels of an explosion inside the heavily fortified Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) that injured three South Korean soldiers, further straining ties on the peninsula.

The game follows several parallel storylines: a squad of young American and South Korean soldiers fighting for survival, a former serviceman driven by revenge, and a power struggle surrounding a new North Korean leader — a character players can also take on.
The new edition has generated considerable interest in South Korea, where able-bodied men are required to serve between 18 and 21 months in the military, depending on the branch.
The title has topped both the global and South Korean sales charts on Steam, one of the world’s largest digital distribution platforms for PC games.
The campaign begins with a surprise invasion of South Korea by North Korean forces, who deploy paratroopers and infiltrate through an underground tunnel to catch South Korean and US troops off guard.
In reality, the US stations about 28,000 troops in South Korea to help deter the nuclear-armed North.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war because the 1950-53 Korean War ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty.

Reactions among South Korean gamers have been largely positive, with some posting hashtags featuring a Korean slogan meaning “exterminate communism” on social media and others saying they were considering upgrading their computers or buying new consoles to play the title.
“I cried so much playing the game to a point I almost got dehydrated. It reminds me so much of my grandfather, who fought in the Korean War,” a Threads user with the handle b_yeol_t said.
Another user, posting under the handle ireozima_zebal, described the experience as “horrifying” because of its implications for a potential conflict on the Korean peninsula.

“This is what would unfold if the North launched an invasion, with the border province of Gangwon overwhelmed within an hour and our defence line pushed back right on the edge of Seoul,” the user said.
But the game has also drawn criticism for turning the fraught history between North and South Korea into entertainment.

The title raises the “question of whether it is appropriate... to present the tragedy of the Korean War and the current antagonism between South and North as something to be consumed for entertainment”, Kim Sung-jae, chairman of the Kim Dae Jung Peace Center, wrote in the Hankyoreh newspaper last month.
On Saturday, North Korean state media said leader Kim Jong Un had urged his military to become the strongest in the world at a two-day meeting of company commanders in Pyongyang last week. — AFP
057c2882eed7c2e0: PARIS, Oct 25 — AFP has deployed reporters, photographers and video journalists in cities across France to document nationwide cost of living protests on Saturday.
Here is a round up of what they are witnessing as security forces seek to prevent a repeat of violence and looting that erupted on the sidelines of similar demonstrations last weekend.
‘Beating up a lot of people’
Police used tear gas and baton charged protesters at the end of the march at Porte de Vincennes on the eastern fringes of Paris.

“The police started moving towards everyone, telling them to get down and back off. They were just taking people down, you know, beating protesters,” said a student, David, who was shaking and bleeding from a gash on his face.
“They were moving really fast and beating up a lot of people. The one of the police officers threw a baton at my face. There was blood everywhere.”
Residents peering out their apartment windows in one classic, Haussmann style building hurriedly slammed them shut and retreated after police fired tear gas near the front door.
‘It makes me sick’
In northern Lille, where the main march began in a calmer atmosphere than last week, protesters chanted “ACAB” — an English language acronym condemning police.

After an hour, the first tear gas canisters plunged part of the march into an opaque, stinging haze. A few projectiles were thrown at police. “We got gassed even though we weren’t doing anything,” said Eline, 23, her eyes full of tears. She said she was demonstrating for the first time.

Appoline, 25, admitted she was “terrified” to join the demonstration, having been shocked by images of police action circulating in recent days. She carried a sign that read: “For all those among us who have been maimed”, a reference to people hurt in recent protests.

“I hesitated to come,” said the psychology student. But “when I see young people losing eyes or hands, it makes me sick,” she whispered, as the Lille procession set off in the rain, accompanied by the beat of techno music.
‘Warzone’

Jeremy Costeweiss, a 21 year old medical student, told AFP he was attending the march in Paris as he feared “things are going to erupt” and he wanted to help people who may get tear gassed or hurt in confrontations.

First responder Alexandre B, speaking to AFP in Paris, described last week’s protests as a “warzone”. He said he had handled seven emergency interventions, including two cases of head trauma and two open fractures.
Saturday’s march was “nothing like” the week before, he added.
Umbrellas and hoods went up as the rain began to intensify over Paris.
‘Don’t do anything stupid’
Several thousand protesters began marching in pouring rain in Bordeaux.
Among them was an older CGT union activist who locked eyes with two masked youths in black tracksuits, and told them: “We’re not here to mess around — don’t do anything stupid.”
At the front of the march, police were nowhere to be seen. “No cops, no problems,” laughed another CGT union member.
Anger
Lucie, a 42 year old designer living in Begles, told AFP at a march in Bordeaux that the violence of last weekend was “unfortunate” but “a form of anger that one can understand”.

“The truth is, if you’ve never known what it’s like to go hungry, to struggle to make ends meet at the end of the month, or to have no idea what your future holds, you can’t truly grasp the kind of anger that can breed,” she said.

Protesters take shelter from a police water cannon near Porte de Vincennes during a nationwide demonstration over rising living costs and public services in Paris on October 24, 2026. — AFP pic
More tear gas
French police fired tear gas in Lyon, Lille, Marseille, Nantes and Toulouse as the protests went on.

Protesters could be seen running as tear gas canisters were launched in Nantes. Police also used a water cannon as they blocked access to a bridge crossing the Loire river, while some demonstrators hurled small projectiles in their direction.
One protester could be seen kicking back a tear gas canister during a demonstration in Toulouse, while another tried to do the same in Lyon.
‘Disappointed’
The only authorised march in Paris began at Porte d’Italie with thousands of people walking in a festive, calm atmosphere beneath cool, overcast skies.
Some carried placards with slogans such as “Macron in the corner” – referring to the French president – and “We expected nothing, yet we’re still disappointed”.

“We’re all here because we want to protest peacefully but people also need to understand that the anger is real. We’ve been walked all over for 10 years,” one protester in a Doctor Who hat who gave their name only as Aurore told AFP.
Ynyane, 19, was dressed as Dragon Ball anime hero Son Goku, a costume he chose “to give people hope”.
“Taxes are a bit too high and I have to support people who are struggling,” he added.
‘I’m also afraid’

High school students who gathered in Toulouse on Saturday spoke of their fears attending a demonstration, after weeks which have seen teenagers wounded and maimed in clashes between police and protesters.

Given the clashes last week and “the repression we faced – which was horrific – I think some people might not be keen on coming today”, 17 year old Ella, a student at the Lycee Marcelin Berthelot in Toulouse, told AFP.
“I’m also afraid of what might happen to me at a protest these days. But the truth is, we can’t give up. Even with this fear, we’re not giving up.”
‘Distressing’
At Porte de Vincennes, where the Paris march finished, some businesses had been barricaded, although many had their shutters down.

“It’s distressing. I don’t know where we’re heading,” said Dominique, an employee at a car rental company who preferred not to give her full name. “My grievance is with the rioters — those who come specifically to smash things and to steal.”
Police are ‘faster’
A 21 year old student protester in Lyon, where demonstrators were tear gassed on Saturday, said police were “highly mobile”.
“We keep moving around but since the police have vehicles, they’re faster. They manage to break up the groups before they can even really form,” he said.
“We end up exchanging information like criminals. We’re in small groups – sometimes just pairs – trying to share updates and find other people, but it’s extremely difficult.”
‘Still open’

Near Paris’s Bastille square, a clothing store removed all its merchandise ahead of the demonstrations, while a nearby restaurant was boarded up despite signs insisting it was “still open”. Many retailers in the capital had wooden boards covering windows.

A heavy police presence could be seen at Bastille, where police used a megaphone to tell the small crowd that the planned demonstration had been banned from the area, ordering protesters to go to the alternate route near Porte d’Italie “immediately”.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A protester lights a flare near Porte de Vincennes during a nationwide demonstration over rising living costs and public services in Paris on October 24, 2026. — AFP pic
Not ‘just one grievance’

“I don’t think the French people have just one grievance,” said Aliyah, 22, sitting with her mother Ludovine at a cafe terrace near the Old Port in Marseille as they waited for demonstrations. She said people’s primary concern was rising costs.

“The people are growing poorer, the people are unhappy, so they take to the streets to protest,” she said, adding that bans on the demonstrations in some cities “only makes us more determined to show up”.
‘Curiosity’
Shops and restaurants were open mid morning in Grenoble — although a curfew was in place in parts of the city and several shopping centres from 6pm.

Francois Xavier Chambron, who works at a bar on the city’s Grenette Square, said they planned to stay open at least for lunch, noting that they already had reservations and that people would be around “out of sheer curiosity”.
Demonstrators gathered for an authorised protest in the afternoon where one participant carried a sign reading: “And so freedom is extinguished under the rain of tear gas”.
‘Hotter than fascists’
Thousands of people yelling anti fascist slogans marched in the city of Orleans against a congress by the far right National Rally (RN) party of Marine Le Pen.
The protest criticised both leading presidential candidate Le Pen and centrist President Emmanuel Macron.
“Macron resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd yelled, carrying placards that read “The Youth say ‘screw you’ to the National Rally” and “Hotter than fascists”.
Tear gas in Lyon
Police fired tear gas to disperse about 150 protesters in the southeastern city of Lyon, in an area banned to all demonstrations.
Police fired several tear gas grenades to clear a group gathered near a university building and the city police station. Police moved in as protesters tried to block a road.

Earlier a police helicopter could be seen flying over the city, with security forces patrolling and armoured vehicles and riot police vans parked nearby. Shops were boarded up, with private security guards in front of some. — AFP
0f2450d462dda48e: NAHAL OZ (Israel), Oct 25 — Danny Rahamim pauses for a few moments as he thinks about his neighbours here on an Israeli kibbutz just a few hundred metres from Gaza.
“I’m probably the most left-wing person here,” he said.

If that was true before October 7, 2023, when Hamas fighters stormed the border and carried out their unprecedented attack, it is even more true today, as Israel readies to vote in its first election since the country’s deadliest ever day.

With a sun-tanned bald head and sporting small glasses, Rahamim has spent 50 of his 72 years here at Nahal Oz, which, like many of Israel’s kibbutzim – small communities in the countryside where all work is shared – has historically reflected the socialist ethos of the country’s founders.
The kibbutzim were once bastions of the left, voting for peace with the Palestinians, but three years ago they found themselves on the frontlines of the Hamas attacks.

Sixteen of Nahal Oz’s 400 residents were killed. Thanks to the proximity of a military base, Rahamim explained, the death toll was significantly lower than at the neighbouring kibbutzim of Kfar Aza, where 64 people died, or Beeri, where 102 died.
“People changed their minds” after the attack, he said.
“Most of them didn’t turn right-wing. But they say they don’t believe anymore that things can get better with our neighbours,” said Rahamim, who serves as the kibbutz’s spokesman.
“I’m not giving up,” he said repeatedly under the flower-covered gazebo of his house.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Danny, a Nahal Oz resident, shows his sunflower tattoo bearing the Hebrew words ‘The Way to Hope’, commemorating the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack, at the kibbutz near the Gaza border on October 22, 2026. — AFP pic
The peace camp has nearly vanished from Israeli politics.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the veteran right-winger whose long career is on the line in Tuesday’s election, has run his campaign on promises of preventing a Palestinian state. His chief opponent, centre-right former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has cast himself as being even more firmly opposed to it.
‘Killing the idea of a better future’
On the walls in Nahal Oz, the bullet holes have disappeared under a fresh coat of paint. But the memories remain ever-present. Rahamim said his own children tell him he is naive.
His grandson, who is almost four, rides his bicycle to the sound of birds chirping.
Above his yard, strewn with oranges that fell from trees, can be heard the constant buzzing of surveillance drones as Israel keeps an eye on the Gaza border.
“It looks quiet. But there were bodies everywhere,” said his stepdaughter, Naama Zadok-Rahamim.
The 37-year-old community employee wears a black T-shirt paying tribute to one of her slain neighbours and a Star of David around her neck. In her eyes, there is anger.
“What I expect from leaders is real security — someone who’s going to make sure that something like this doesn’t happen again,” she said.
During previous cycles of violence, when she heard the bombs falling on the other side of the border, she thought of the suffering of her “neighbours”.
“Now it’s hard for me to make the separation between Hamas and the other population. I don’t know if there’s much difference,” she said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Israeli right-wing members of the Nachala settler organisation are seen at a newly built camp site at a field near the Israeli Kibbutz of Nahal Oz in southern Israel, by the Israel-Gaza border on October 22, 2026. — AFP pic
Nadav Perez, a 44-year-old hospital worker, has always voted for the left or the far left.
Before the attack, he was involved in a project to build a clinic for patients from Gaza. The regional council official behind the initiative was killed defending his kibbutz in Kfar Aza.
“I wondered if the terrorists who killed him knew that their bullets were killing the idea of a better future,” Perez said.
Since then, “my compassion is more blurred,” he admitted, his one-year-old son in his arms.
“I’m sorry to say it,” he said, “but I don’t really care what’s happening on the other side.”
He said he had not decided how to vote in Tuesday’s election. But he will not vote for Netanyahu, angry he has not taken responsibility for the failure to prevent the October 7 attack.
Ruins nearby

Danny Rahamim, for his part, will vote for the centre-left candidate Yair Golan, noting that he is the only major party leader who has made clear he would govern with lawmakers from Israel’s Arab minority.
Looking out on Gaza from an observation post, he pointed to the fences that were so easily breached on October 7.
What once were the first houses on the Gaza side, just 750 metres (820 yards) away, are now nothing but rubble. In the distance, Gaza City also lies in ruins and a burst of gunfire rings out.

9f4e4fe04afae328: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 25 — Palm oil blended in Malaysia must carry accurate declarations of origin, as any inaccuracy could undermine the integrity and reputation of Malaysian products in international markets, a maritime expert said.

Universiti Malaysia Terengganu (UMT) Faculty of Maritime Studies senior lecturer Dr Madzli Harun said that while palm oil blending was permitted in the industry, the process did not automatically make the finished product Malaysian in origin.

He said a product’s country of origin was determined under the applicable Rules of Origin (RoO), which take into account processing methods, raw material content and criteria set out under the relevant trade regulations.

“If the original bill of lading (B/L) states that the refined, bleached and deodorised (RBD) palm olein originates from Indonesia, subsequently blending the product in Malaysia does not automatically make it a Malaysian-origin product.

“The B/L may be amended after a vessel leaves the port of loading and while it is sailing to the port of destination, but such amendments must be supported by reasonable grounds and valid documentation,” he said.

Madzli said blending alone might not satisfy RoO requirements or change a product’s country of origin, and operators must therefore show that the processing carried out meets the relevant criteria before the finished product can be declared Malaysian in origin.
“In the Asean context, the Asean Trade in Goods Agreement (Atiga) sets out rules of origin that include criteria such as Regional Value Content (RVC), change in tariff classification and cumulation.

“The use of raw materials from Asean member states may be taken into account when determining the origin of a finished product under certain circumstances, subject to the requirements of the agreement.

“Operators cannot simply blend oil from Indonesia with Malaysian oil and then label it ‘Made in Malaysia’. The finished product must meet the prescribed requirements before it can qualify for recognition as Malaysian-origin,” he said.

He said the Royal Malaysian Customs Department (RMCD), the Malaysian Palm Oil Board (MPOB) and the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (Miti) should examine the relevant documentation within their respective jurisdictions to ensure blending activities and origin declarations complied with the applicable regulations.
“The documents that need to be examined include import and export records, certificates of origin, the quantity of imported oil, the volume of Malaysian oil used and records of the blending process.
“Traceability is also important to ensure that the origin of raw materials can be identified even after products from different countries have been blended.

“Even if the finished product qualifies for Malaysian-origin status under the applicable rules, records of raw materials imported from Indonesia must still be retained. Information on the origin of those materials must not simply be erased after blending,” he said.

He also warned that if a blended product was found to be contaminated, Malaysia could suffer reputational damage, face cargo rejections by buyers and potentially encounter legal action, depending on the circumstances and the parties responsible.
Madzli said false declarations could also lead to action under the relevant laws, including Section 133 of the Customs Act 1967, if the elements of an offence under the provision were established.

Meanwhile, maritime expert Prof Nazery Khalid said documentation for blended cargoes should accurately reflect the composition and characteristics of the resulting product to avoid doubts about its contents.

He said this was important because if a blended cargo was found to be contaminated and posed a health risk to consumers after export, Malaysia could suffer reputational damage if the product was perceived to have originated from the country.
“The recent food poisoning incident in Taiwan involving contaminated cooking oil should serve as a lesson.

“As one of the world’s major palm oil producers, Malaysia must ensure that its exported oil meets quality and integrity standards, while ensuring that its processing, documentation and shipment are carried out properly,” he said.

MOH is also expanding access to mental health services through 1,116 government health clinics nationwide, in addition to hospitals and community-based services such as Community Mental Health Centres (MENTARI).
He noted that there are approximately 700 registered psychiatrists in Malaysia, with 400 serving within

9c43fb825ff142a7: TEHRAN, Oct 25 — Iran’s parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Sunday called for a campaign to cut gas consumption by at least 10 per cent, with officials anticipating shortages as winter approaches.

While a major producer, Iran has long suffered shortages of natural gas, essential for powering heating systems, which have been exacerbated by war with the United States and Israel that began in February.
During the most intense phase of the fighting, which lasted nearly 40 days, the two countries struck key Iranian infrastructure including natural gas refineries, according to Tehran.
Winter in Iran often sees temperatures drop below freezing, especially in the country’s north.
“To get through the approaching winter, a nationwide effort is essential ... to reduce gas consumption by at least 10 per cent,” said Ghalibaf in a video carried by Iranian media.

“Anyone who saves gas, regardless of the amount, will immediately receive the corresponding proceeds in their bank account, allowing everyone to see the tangible impact of those savings on their household budget.”

Earlier in October, First Vice-President Mohammad Reza Aref said the government anticipated a daily “gas shortfall of 100 million to 250 million cubic metres during the cold season because of the damage caused by the war,” according to the official IRNA news agency.
He added that he hoped to restore the supply of around 100 million cubic metres by the start of winter.

An April ceasefire brought an end to the initial phase of intense bombardment but the two sides have continued to vie for control over the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas used to travel.
Iran has claimed control over the strait since the outbreak of the war and has regularly targeted vessels that attempt crossings without its authorisation.

In response, Washington has imposed a counter-blockade on Iranian ports and in August announced what it called an “economic asphyxiation” campaign on Iran aimed at strangling its already battered economy. — AFP

38f83d736152635d: RIYADH, Oct 25 — Yemen’s Houthis launched wide-ranging strikes across swathes of southern Saudi Arabia on Sunday, as the kingdom announced the partial reopening of Riyadh international airport despite repeated attacks by the group.

Alerts warning of possible attacks were activated across the kingdom’s south throughout the day, with the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis saying at least 10 ballistic missiles were intercepted.
Saudi Arabia, which leads a military coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis, has faced a barrage of strikes from the group in recent weeks.
The fighting erupted after a years-long truce between the Houthis and Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government fell apart.
“The bombardment has been very heavy since this morning — may God keep us safe.
“Everything is shaking because of the explosions,” one resident in Khamis Mushait told AFP Sunday on condition of anonymity.
Further north, Riyadh’s international airport said flights would resume on Sunday after a two-week closure following the Houthi strikes.
However it remained unclear to what extent the airport was operational.

The Houthi fighters have carried out waves of strikes on the airport, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
The group has also targeted oil infrastructure and other sites.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that Riyadh airport was still “unsafe” and a “military target”.

“The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional and local airlines – as well as staff and travellers – against using King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces,” he said.
“The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport.”
Attack warning

As the airport prepared to open, AFP journalists in Riyadh heard three explosions in the early hours of Sunday, with residents receiving alert messages for a “hostile aerial threat” urging them to stay in a safe place.
The warning came as the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had downed a ballistic missile launched by the group towards the capital, as well as two drones in the capital area.
“Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh,” the coalition posted on X.
Later Sunday morning, the coalition said its forces intercepted a cruise missile fired by the Houthis at the kingdom’s southern city of Khamis Mushait.
Attacks appeared to target areas across the south, with warnings also issued for Abha city along with areas in Taif, Namas and Jazan.
The attacks came after the Houthi fighters said that – in the space of 24 hours – they targeted three Saudi airports, including in Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an air base.
The Saudi civil defence agency said it had also responded to falling debris in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday after intercepting two Houthi missiles.
The Houthis denied targeting the cities, the two holiest in Islam, calling the Saudi claim a “huge lie”.
The Houthis also fired at the southern Yemeni city of Aden, the interim seat of the Saudi-backed government, saying they targeted a naval base and military camp overseen by Saudi forces.
The flare-up in Yemen, with the Houthis taking control of the entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive last month, has further destabilised the region and disrupted oil markets.

The Houthi attacks have dealt a blow to Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest exporter of crude, disrupting businesses, airlines and residents, and rattling its drive to shift its international image. — AFP

cf7dae3c81ea803e: Building a UK datacenter spans three government departments: one handles datacenter policy, another telecoms, and a third energy.
MPs this week explored what Prime Minister Andy Burnham's summer reshuffle means for businesses navigating Whitehall.

Liz Lloyd, parliamentary under-secretary of state, sits across two departments with a portfolio of responsibilities as long as a weekly shopping list. She explained to MPs this week that, following the decision to get rid of the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), liaison with the tech industry on datacenter construction fell to the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST).
Lloyd, who works across BIST and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), went on to explain that digital infrastructure sits within DCMS.
Speaking to the House of Commons Science and Technology Committee, Lloyd acknowledged that some departmental responsibilities overlapped.

"In terms of sector responsibilities, that is clear that technology, sorry, that telecom sits with DCMS and datacenters with BIST. When you're actually in an industry or you're trying to run a business, that that that is clear," the junior minister said.

Any business trying to build a datacenter might also want to know how to get power to it. As far as The Register can figure out, that would be the Department for Energy and Net Zero. Planning permission rests with local government, although the overall policy lies with the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. It may be clear, but it is hardly simple.
The problem is real, though. Earlier this month, Microsoft pulled out of plans for Britain's largest AI supercomputer because of difficulties securing power for the facility.
Elsewhere in the hearing, Lloyd was asked about the government's early 2025 claim that modernizing aging technology and digitizing processes could deliver £45 billion in productivity savings.

Asked if the government stood by the figure, the junior minister said: "The £45 billion figure was an estimate of long-term productivity gains. It wasn't a kind of one-off figure for savings… it was never a figure that was a target or a cashable savings figure."

When the figure was publicized under the Starmer government in January 2025, the press release was headed "Archaic tech sees public sector miss £45 billion annual savings." It continued: "Taxpayer funded services from the NHS to local councils are missing out on £45 billion in productivity savings because they are too often dependent on old and outdated technology."
It claimed the government would "tackle these issues" using "digital tools, AI and common sense to overhaul public sector technology." ®

50937a197e15b8bf: TOKYO, Oct 25 — Japanese automakers are stepping up efforts to shorten their vehicle development times as they seek to catch up with Chinese rivals that offer new models to global markets more quickly and to better respond to changing customer demand, Kyodo News reported.

Toyota Motor Corp, Honda Motor Co, Nissan Motor Co and other Japanese carmakers typically spend around four to five years developing a new model, more than twice as long as the less than two years taken by Chinese companies.
As part of its reform measures, Nissan aims to slash development times under its new family-based vehicle development strategy.
The carmaker will design a common platform for multiple models of the same size.
The carmaker, for example, plans to shorten the lead time for developing a new sport-utility vehicle model to three years and one month for launch in North America in 2028.
It will then use the same platform as that of the new SUV for its derivative models, enabling it to reduce development time by up to 40 per cent to two and a half years.
The new product strategy will cover 80 per cent of the company’s global sales and is expected to cut the number of part types by 70 per cent.
“This is a reform to become a company that responds to changes and delivers good cars in a timely manner,” Hidemi Sasaki, deputy general manager of Nissan’s product planning division, said.

Honda, seeking a V-shaped recovery from its first net loss in the last fiscal year, has introduced the “Triple Half” approach designed to halve development costs, time frames and workloads from 2025 levels, making full use of artificial intelligence and other digital technologies.
The new initiatives will begin with new models whose development the company will start in 2028.
Toyota, the world’s largest automaker by volume, is also working to reduce types of parts, depending on customer needs, as fewer parts will improve productivity and speed up development work.
Naming the project “Area 35”, Toyota aims to improve the use of plant floor space by 35 per cent.

Suzuki Motor Corp. plans to halve its current development time to around two years, while Mitsubishi Motors Corp also aims to shorten the period by 20 per cent to three years by around 2030. — Bernama-Kyodo
0efd9cf003b3b02d: Gender diversity, resistance and ritual cross-dressing in Venezuela's sacred cult
Originally published on Global Voices

Portrait of Wander Rodríguez, part of the María Dolores Rodríguez Caravan and its powers, and the LGBTIQ+ community. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

In Venezuela, Spiritism as a religion is part of the collective imagination, of our identity; popular beliefs and ritual practices that take us back to our ancestors in colonial times. Over the years, Spiritism has evolved into a vibrant, contemporary national cult centered on the figure of María Lionza as the principal protector of waters and the charms of nature, a figure who challenges the notions of the patriarchal state and opposes monotheistic religions.

This religious system has been studied in depth by anthropologists in our country (Daisy Barreto, Angelina Pollak-Eltz, Michelle Asencio, Francisco Ferrándiz, Cesar Escalona, among others), which I had read about and found interesting at the time, but which I later witnessed for the first time in its most important sites, such as Quibayo and Sorte, in the state of Yaracuy, Venezuela.
Altar to María Lionza in Quibayo (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 11. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

These sites are part of the Cerro María Lionza Natural Monument, popularly known as the Montaña de Sorte, and they represent the most prominent expressions of this cult nationwide, so they are visited year-round by practitioners or “caravans” (as these groups are commonly called),
But few days are as important as October 11 and 12, when thousands of people flock there to celebrate the Day of Indigenous Resistance in Venezuela.

These dates offer an opportunity for ethnographic and cultural observation, specifically how oral histories and our ethnic origins are reclaimed; including those of Indigenous peoples, some of them warriors who fought against Spanish colonization, and African populations — enslaved people and maroons [AN: this will need context] — as we can understand through the figure of the Three Powers: Queen María Lionza as the central figure of the cult, the leader, accompanied by El Indio Guaicaipuro and El Negro Felipe.
Altar to Queen María Lionza in Quibayo (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 11. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

For this celebration families gather among the trees and along the banks of the Yaracuy River, which runs through the entire mountain, setting up lavish altars to the various deities of Venezuelan spiritualism, which embody the sacred rituals characteristic of the Marialioncero cult.

The figure of María Lionza is profound, and I believe it is risky to oversimplify her, as she is regarded as a Queen, a Goddess, a mother, and a guardian, yet there are also aspects linked to her sensuality, as evidenced by the iconographic representations of her that have emerged -naked or clothed, for example-.

In this regard, I draw upon the writings of Francisco Ferrándiz and César Escalona from the perspective of Venezuelan anthropology, combining them with my own observations and field interviews, to address issues related to gender and sexual diversity that are essential to the fascinating debate within the cult on its various courts — such as the Black Court, the Viking Court, the Malandra Court, the Chamarrera Court, and the Medical Court, among others — and entities.
Detail of flowers and bottles of the Baile del vidrio (Glass Dance Ritual) in Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.
Gender diversity, gender discrimination

The Sorte Mountain is a setting where gender stereotypes are called into question, and I believe they undermine androcentric perspectives and rigid notions of masculinity and femininity found within Christianity, since the entities pose a challenge due to their wide spectrum in terms of strength, height, voice, attire, and other details of the mediums who embody them, as well as the particular characteristics of each spirit.
Strenght between banks and Viking Court entity. Baile del vidrio (Glass Dance Ritual) in Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

In his ethnographies and writings, Ferrandíz offers interesting reflections on the body and masculinity in this religion, and how male mediums (from a position of stigmatized masculinity) resisted possession by female spirits, something that did not occur as frequently among female spiritualists.
That is why my encounter in Sorte with the María Dolores Rodríguez Caravan and its powers — led by Osmer Padrón and his godchildren — allowed me to also explore these aspects.
Osmer Padrón embodies the spirit of María Dolores. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

Osmer Padrón, Wander Rodríguez, and Jhonaiker Díaz are all male mediums that belong to the LGBTQ+ community, and are part of this caravan that channels female entities from the Black Court, such as María Dolores Rodríguez, Francisca Martínez, Rita Encarnación, and La Negra Tomasa; but in Osmer’s case, he also channels Mister Piter, a male entity from the Viking Court, a warrior and healer.

Wander tells me that in the LGBTQ+ spiritualist community, “there’s a lot of discrimination, both inside and outside the mountain [of Sorte], but Queen María Lionza is love and affection, and as many spiritual beings have said, we are all deeply cherished by her. We are here first and foremost to fulfill a mandate from Goddess and our Majesty María Lionza. Nothing else matters.”

Portraits of Jhonaiker Díaz (who works with the spirit of La Negra Tomasa) and José Rojas. They are part of the LGBTIQ+ community. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.
Regarding the practice of channeling female entities from the Black Court, Rodríguez tells me:

Most of us spiritualists in the LGBTQ+ community dress up in dresses — or find ourselves transported into that state — not because we want to… Right now, there’s a lot of talk from people saying that men who want to be women channel Black Court entities just to wear dresses, but that’s not the case. When a spiritual entity is a woman or was a woman, she always seeks to be fully covered, to cover her breasts, and why? Because she feels exposed; she feels alive. There are many spiritual entities, such as the Negra I work with — who is Rita Encarnación Martínez Chávez — as well as María Dolores Rodríguez Rodríguez, Francisca Martínez Martínez, and Negra Tomasa, who have their dresses made for them. It’s not because we want to wear dresses; if they were our own bodies, we’d walk around shirtless, but no, they always… Spirituality always seeks to feel alive; that’s why they put on their dress, their turban, and some even seek out a flower.

Dresses for female entities from the Black Court: Francisca Martínez, Francisca Palacios, María Dolores Rodríguez, Negra Tomasa and Rita Encarnación. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

There are curious details regarding what the entities ask of their “banks” —people who also care for the physical forms of the entities — such as tobacco and aguardiente; but in the case of the black women, just as they ask for their dresses, they also ask for makeup and make gestures as if looking at themselves in a mirror.

Wander tells me that, in the case of Rita Encarnación, “her favorite flower is the cayena, since it was the flower with which she learned to perform her magic, while she labels “other flowers as hypocrites, since those other flowers remain alive for many days after being plucked from nature, whereas the cayena once plucked from nature wilt immediately.”
Altar to Las Tres Potencias (The Three Powers), in Quibayo (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 11. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.

All of this demonstrates that Venezuelan spiritism must be examined through a gender lens, from a feminist perspective, reflecting on the power dynamics established between men and women, the presence of ritual cross-dressing during trance and possession rituals, and other aspects that enrich our understanding of this important Venezuelan religion.
Wander Rodríguez enters a trance to receive the spirit of Rita Encarnación. Sorte (Yaracuy, Venezuela). October 12. Freisy González Portales. Used with permission.
Written by Freisy González
